#108940. Breaking: Inside Retro Reset, the "really inspirational" father and son project teaching kids about classic games hardware from aboard a converted bus

Breaking: Inside Retro Reset, the "really inspirational" father and son project teaching kids about classic games hardware from aboard a converted bus

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that at first the kids jostle to get to the games that they know.
  • Luke’s knowledge is beautiful but the students also find him approachable.
  • Industry observers note that the bleeps and blips start from the machines as the students start playing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that at first the kids jostle to get to the games that they know. "Welcome to the Retro Reset Bus," states Luke Stoner as the students push to get to the screen that’s caught their eye. Sonic on the Sega Mega Drive is the first they see, and the quickest student to get on board the bus looks triumphant as he nabs the stool in front of the console. Jason, Luke’s dad, asks him what he thinks about the graphics – slightly grainy and slightly pixelated – but he’s not at all bothered and soon engrossed. After a few minutes, though, his eyes keep moving to the back of the bus where "Jackson is a wally" is now emblazoned across a flickering screen in seven different colours. Jackson then gives out a chuffed yell when his code finally works after a couple of restarts. His retort to his mate appears on the 1981 BBC Micro Model B‘s screen as the other students crane to have a look. This is, incidentally, the machine that turned a national broadcaster into a computer retailer (with help from Acorn), says Jason.

Luke’s knowledge is beautiful but the students also find him approachable. As Jason shares: "It’s really inspirational for kids coming onto a bus that they can talk to someone younger like Luke, who knows his stuff and has made something incredible happen." One student asks where Minecraft is and Luke explains that it doesn’t fit the parameter of being more than twenty years old yet, sharing details of when it was published and by who. Roblox could be included, but Luke isn’t keen because of recent controversies around safety. When this group are reluctantly herded off the bus by even more reluctant teachers, another heads in with just a little gap for resetting the machines and cramming a biscuit.

Industry observers note that the bleeps and blips start from the machines as the students start playing. One teacher stops at the Atari 2600 and shares that her family has just bought her one. She is loving the daily dose of nostalgia. Luke and Jason move up and down the bus answering questions, resetting machines and showing the students their collection of old phones. One student winces at he is passed the bag that would have carried the battery for a Panasonic EB-3600 "brick" phone from 1989. When Jason states his dad had one, they give that look of pity reserved for anyone over 30 but are also incredulous that anyone would lug that around, especially when the phone could only do calls. When Jason asks if anyone would like to break an iPhone and have a look inside, all of the hands shoot up. He then talks about memory, RAM and chips, brings out a floppy disk; and tells the tale of where the expression "computer bug" came from. Still, it's the game on a tape - Jungle Story for the Commodore 64 - which they all turn away from screens to see. Perhaps we have Stranger Things to thank, but the tape has retro currency and they all think it’s sick.

Sources indicate that the event is being run by East Sussex Careers Hub and is specifically aimed at students with SEND (Special Educational Needs and Disabilities). More than twenty-five schools turn up and most teachers leave with a flyer, chatting to colleagues about where the bus could park onsite. Jason says that the response to the bus, since Retro Reset's launch as a registered charity in August 2025, has been phenomenal, and they could easily fill a full week with visits. For now, he is juggling it with work commitments.

Industry observers note that the bus was Luke’s idea and inspired by a visit to The Centre for Computing History in Cambridge, where visitors can get their hands on home computers and consoles from decades gone by. The family started thinking about what was possible and finally, after Luke finished college, began kitting out the bus: buying or accepting donations of hardware, researching which monitors would work with the ancient systems, and installing it all within the cabin.

On a basic level, the charity is telling the story of how technology has iterated. But by allowing visitors to take apart their machines, and giving brief lessons in coding with Basic, it also pulls the veil back on the work that goes into making a game - while opening students' eyes to what they could create themselves. "I guess it’s bridging the gap between the polished and finished latest game," Jason notes, "which could be perceived as not achievable for them, to seeing how all that coding came about. Other than making sure they are really accurate with their typing; they realise that coding can be quite simple and something that they can actually do. I would go further and say that when they have written some code, nearly all of them have a significant smile on their face." This, he hopes, might be the spark for some students to get into coding, especially for PC games, where under-18s are an underrepresented demographic.

It also hit the road as the popularity of retro gaming continued to surge. According to a Consumer Reports survey published last February, 14% of US gamers regularly play games made before 2000. This is reflected in the staggering stat that the retro gaming market is estimated to be worth $3.8 billion globally, with a projected rise to $8 billion by 2033. Retro-focused videos on YouTube and TikTok rack up millions of views of views, and communities formed on reddit or Discord - some with hundreds of thousands of members - discuss nothing else.

Nostalgia is playing a huge part. Atari’s Implicit Conversations is built on just this, creating retro games for modern consoles like PlayStation 5 or the Nintendo Switch. For Luke, though, this misses the point. He likes the click when you put a cartridge in a machine; and he likes that he is just him and the game. The parents of visiting students appreciate this too, and often share how overwhelming it feels to keep their kids safe in the online gaming environment. "Parents of younger children [tell us that] they hate that Minecraft and Roblox can allow their kids to play against perceived strangers. Even the more technical parents say they still miss safety measures and would prefer the games not be online at all," Jason explains.

According to recent reports, last month, Ofcom published its Growing Up Gaming summary report, which found that almost two-thirds (64%) of parents of three to 17 year olds who game online are concerned about their child talking to strangers through games or their chat functions. And, while the vast majority of young players go online without incident, it is true that those who use chat functions will likely interact with strangers. The same research found that more than half (55%) of children who game online say they play with people they have never met offline at least sometimes, while one in five (20%) do so all or most of the time they play.

Recent findings suggest that by contrast, Jason claims that not one student has asked if they can get online, and he’s also never seen one get out their phone when they’re on the bus. Perhaps it is a welcomed break. "We offer a completely safe environment to come and experience these games and machines. That's really what we're here for," he states.

Luke shares too that he became nervous of the data he was sharing with gaming companies, and conscious that this was all being stored, thus making it vulnerable to breaches. He also baulked at what he felt was a constant money grab from gaming companies, including moves that render games unsupported or completely obsolete. Retro gaming is cheap in comparison and therefore more accessible, especially for younger players. "When you tell them that they can get an old console for less than £100 and often games come free when you buy them second hand, their ears really prick up," Jason says. "For a lot of the youngsters, the cost of modern gaming equipment is unattainable. And of course, we explain that they could take old computers and laptops and then load free operating software onto them. This gets them online, often for free. Once they are there, they can game.".

John W. Champeau is founder of Champ Games, a Connecticut-based venture, which develops retro games system primarily for the Atari 2600. He has Scramble, Galagon, Gorf Arcade and Elevator Agent on his line-up. He agrees that price point is a huge part of the appeal of retro gaming. "Atari has released a line of "+" systems that are modern reinterpretations of the class Atari 2600 and 7800 hardware, but at a lower price point but with modern conveniences such as HDMI support, firmware updates, and fresh controllers," he notes. These systems can also play older cartridges that were released back in the day. "This means that the games themselves can be acquired at a low cost as well, sometimes even free if someone is lucky enough to know someone with a box of old Atari carts in their basement or attic.".

According to recent reports, but there may also be something intrinsically different about how these games are designed to be played that is driving their renaissance. In December 2025, Newsweek shared the views of two mental health professionals that "90s Video Games Were Better for Kids’ Brains." In what was sure to be a contentious piece (and perhaps that was the point), mental health counsellor Veronica Lichtenstein, and Melissa Gallagher, a licensed clinical social worker, argued that the very nature of gaming has changed and is now damaging. Retro games had a start and an end – and with the latter came a major hit of dopamine for achieving victory. Modern games are designed as "loops for addiction" with no real end; and constant prompts to buy. Satisfaction is constantly deferred. Lichtenstein also says that modern games leave little room for critical thinking, as a quick search online will delivers solutions if a player ever gets stuck.

Champeau agrees. "Our games are not designed to be addictive 'time stealers' like some modern video games that encourage players to 'stay online' for hours on end to acquire additional resources needed to complete a game or advance to a new level, etc," he states, adding: "All of our games are designed to be short burst distractions that don't rely on long gaming sessions to feel a sense of accomplishment.” He says that the lower graphics resolution and primitive sounds are actually a relief for many after years of hyper-realistic gaming. "Retro games distance the gap between game and reality, which was the intention of video games in the first place," he argues.

In a recent development, back on the bus, Sonic may have attracted the initial crowds but it is now Pacman and the Binatone that the students are huddling around. Jason has given up one control for the tennis game to a student and a noisy competition is now taking place. The graphics are basic as is the premise, but scoring is tricky and the battle to get to 15 points hard-fought. The teacher laughs. "The bleeps from that game are bringing back memories," she notes as she tries to encourage her students to finish and hand over the controllers. But with faces lit up by the screen and set in concentration, they don’t hear her. This is play for play’s sake, with no distractions, and could be why the games of the past might be just the future these kids need.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the cars Randy wants in GTA 6 is the Ocelot Bloodless Jugular—and don't let the name fool you, its a slick and speedy ride that'll you'll be tempted to keep for yourself.

According to recent reports, but Randy doesn't know the locations of many of the cars on his wishlist, and can't point you to the Ocelot Bloodless Jugular: you just need to keep an eye out for it. Luckily, we spotted it ourselves, so just follow the simple steps below to find it.

Head to Belville: It's a town in Leonard County, in the central eastern part of the map, a bit south of Lake Leonida and north of La Perle.

It has been revealed that in the northern edge of Belville there's a little cluster of four homes laid out almost in an X pattern. The southernmost home of that cluster has a garage you can break into. Once you open the garage door, you'll see the white Ocelot Bloodless Jugular.

Sources indicate that you'll need the key cloner to get in, which I assume you already have since you're doing jobs for Randy. No need to worry about the tracker, it's a standard one so it won't transmit your location to the cops. You still don't want to dawdle, because the owner of the car has a gun and he's not afraid to use it. He'll start shooting if he sees you boost the car.

In a recent development, randy will pay you $10,615 for the Ocelot Bloodless Jugular. He'll pay an extra $5,000 if you bring it to him in pristine condition.

  • It has been revealed that the trailer, which covers the Commander Edition of Dawn of War 4, includes a breakdown of all the extra stuff packed in alongside this version of the game.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Dawn of War 4's December release date inches ever closer, a new trailer appears to have teased a fan-favourite character's inclusion in the RTS's first post-launch DLC.

It has been revealed that the trailer, which covers the Commander Edition of Dawn of War 4, includes a breakdown of all the extra stuff packed in alongside this version of the game. This includes the digital soundtrack, three-days of early-access to the game, and the story prologue. It'll also include the Aftermath post-launch DLC too, with its dedicated campaign and new playable faction.

Now, ever since the Aftermath DLC was announced, people have speculated it would be chaos-focused. The design of the DLC logo is black with a gold trim, an often-used colour scheme for the faction. However, which sort of Chaos was left up to debate. That is, until this trailer, where the answer is seemingly given away with a cheeky tease.

Sources indicate that in its final few seconds, the trailer demonstrates a pair of glowing yellow mechanical eyes peering out from a gloomy background. This was swiftly identified as almost-certainly Vashtorr the Arkifane, a relatively newly introduced addition to Warhammer 40,000 and a fan-favourite baddie all around.

Vashtorr as a character has been getting a lot of love ever since his introduction in 2023. It was then, during the Arks of Omen campaign for the tabletop game, that he played a central part in the narrative event bridging the game's 10th and 11th edition. Since then he was the main antagonist of Boltgun 2, and was central in the 2025 novel Achmagos.

According to recent reports, what this means for Dawn of War 4 is that, if he is a commander of Chaos forces, expect a lot of machinery and demon engines on his side. That's kind of his whole deal. Whether that means he's paired with tech-focused Dark Mechanicum as a sort of mirror to the Adeptus Mechanicus faction already in the game, or if he'll come alongside Chaos Space Marines to better reflect the Dark Angels / Blood Ravens remains to be seen. It could also be a mix of both! We'll have to wait and see.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After appearing in both God of War Ragnarok and next year's God of War Laufey, Deborah Ann Woll is about to reprise her role as Faye in Amazon Prime Video's upcoming live-action series.

Industry observers note that variety reports that the God of War cast list is now welcoming a second actor pulled straight from Sony Santa Monica's video game series. Deborah Ann Woll first showed up in the games as Kratos' wife and Atreus' mother during God of War Ragnarok, but she's also about to enter the spotlight proper in God of War Laufey.

Industry observers note that amazon's God of War cast now includes Dave Bautista (Guardians of the Galaxy) as god killer Kratos, Callum Vinson (Chucky) as Atreus, Mandy Patinkin as Odin and Ólafur Darri Ólafsson as Thor. Alastair Duncan is also making the game-to-show jump by stepping back into the figurative shoes of chatty head Mimir.

According to recent reports, earlier in the year, the God of War show halted production when former Kratos actor Ryan Hurst suffered an on-set injury. Bautista soon took over the role and production began again in October - all of Hurst's scenes had to be reshot, of course.

Recent findings suggest that there's no release date yet for the show, but it's mentioned to follow the Norse era of the games which began in 2018's more serious and stern revamp. Amazon ordered a two-season run for the show, which apparently means both seasons will be filmed back-to-back.

Meanwhile, God of War Laufey was recently delayed from February 2027 to May 2027, giving the PS5 exclusive slightly more breathing room away from Fable, Persona 4 Revival and Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis.

"We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential," developer Sony Santa Monica remarked at the time. "On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we'll be back to share more updates soon.".

Recent findings suggest that while the game puts Faye in the leading role as she battles with gods in a multi-mythological afterlife, the studio was quick to note that her journey isn't considered a side game. God of War Laufey will still connect to future games in the series and, yep, Kratos will eventually be back, too.

Industry observers note that "Genuinely, I thought I was going to be much more offended by it, but one, I'm not on social media, so that helps, and two, I don't know, I feel totally unbothered," Woll stated of the online trolls who were targeting Laufey after its reveal this summer. "Because I just know it's great. It's okay if it's not your cup of tea, but in no universe is it bad.".

Sources indicate that to be fair, I’ve made no secret of my plans to do just that if you’ve read any of our recent roundups of what everyone’s playing over the weekend. I can understand why it might leave a sour taste in the mouth, but it is what it is. No corporate gun has been pointed at my head as a mandate to temporarily forsake my PC and play the substantial game of the moment is forced into my hands.

Anyway, I’m writing about playing GTA 6 on console because it’s led me to conclude that a particular aspect of GTA 5’s PC port - one I’ve always rather taken for granted - could be a bigger deal for the inevitable Windows version of 6 than even the usual go-to PC plus points. You know, better graphics, superior performance, and modding. Historically, Rockstar’s crime sandboxes are games played from the third person perspective. That shot lingering behind Niko Bellic as he jogs around Brooklyn with a rocket launcher or following the damn bike of CJ as he in turn follows that damn train. This is the default way GTA’s breakneck action is presented to the player and was with GTA 5 at launch.

As Rockstar’s offerings have shuffled away from arcadey rampage facilitators and ever deeper into the mould of uber-detailed life of crime sims, however, they've also began letting players see things directly through the eyes of the crim whose blood-splattered shoes they’ve stepped into. In order to do that, while simultaneously pushing the detail and graphical boundaries of their rendered worlds, Rockstar have needed to squeeze every bit of juice they can from the available hardware. Red Dead Redemption 2 managed to include a full first person mode at launch. GTA 6 hasn’t been so lucky, even if there are moments when bringing up your phone or reading a note temporarily lodges the camera into Jason and Lucia’s noggins.

There is a way to glitch yourself into a more permanent first person perspective, but it’s naturally not got the polish that a proper first person mode would. What it does do is make clear that, with vehicle interiors lavishly detailed and some gun animations looking natural rather than janky, any port using the PC's extra horses to deliver a proper first person mode seems a no brainer, if not something already set in stone.

In a recent development, assuming that is the case, I frankly can’t see why first person won’t become the go-to perspective on PC. Even more so than RDR2, GTA 6 feels like a game built to belong in first person. It dedicates so much time and energy to engaging you in every aspect of Jason and Lucia’s routines, rendering everything from eating to working out to doing up a house (and the acts involved in doing a robbery, I guess) in such exhaustive detail and depth that it’s almost beyond parody.

Sources indicate that notifications ping about you needing to finish a bench pressing session where every rep involves holding and releasing R2 and L2 at just the right time. An app tells you you’re hungry, so you wander over to the fridge, pick out a protein shake to down, then press R2 to lob the bottle in the bin, assuming you’re keen to keep your flat tidy. Shopping trips see you pick up groceries off shelves, stow them in a bag, then run home with it tucked under your arm because you’ve brought a motorbike and forgotten it lacks a boot. Every stickup begins with the ritual of picking your longarm gun out of your car’s boot, where it might have sat next to a bag of drugs you’ve stowed to deliver to a fence later. Stopping off to switch cars and clothes to throw the cops off your scent is no longer just for overenthusiastic roleplayers.

Recent findings suggest that the fact that the game goes to such lengths only to maintain the detachment inherent to the third person view feels bizarrely antithetical at times, like an exhibition of a tiny Fabergé egg that you’re forced to view through a telescope from the surface of Mars. The massive efforts of Rockstar’s developers - many of whom are currently trying to gain formal union recognition or have been fighting the company at an employment tribunal over firings they argue were unjust - went into putting together an artwork that regularly ends up at an arm’s length out of necessity, despite packing intricacies likely best seen through a magnifying glass.

Enter the PC release. And possibly nothing else offering the same bang for your buck around the same time. With GTA 5, the PS4 and Xbox One got an enhanced version of the game around the time of the PC port, offering a number of extra features - including a first person mode. Rockstar were quick to rule out GTA 6 getting 60 or 40fps performance modes on current console hardware due to a lack of horses, and if that also applies to a first person mode, then such a thing might only come with the next generation of consoles. That’d be the PS6 and Xbox’s Project Helix, neither of which seem hugely imminent and could well end up boasting ludicrous prices thanks to the ongoing memory shortages.

According to recent reports, so, those who already own a PC capable of running any GTA 6 port could be in the best position to enjoy the game from a Jason and Lucia-eye view the moment such a thing becomes possible. Sure, it would also look and run better, but to be brutally honest I’ve found it looks damn gorgeous and runs acceptably on PS5. Sure, modding will no doubt spring up must-have additions, but the base game already works in plenty of the roleplaying mechanics and in-depth side-jobbing that a lot of popular GTA 5 mods delivered.

In a recent development, thus, that window as the place to play GTA 6 as it feels intended, in first person, is what I’d currently peg as the best chance for the crimsim to be not just a great game you can play on PC - as I’d argue Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA 5 are - but a great PC game that’s inarguably best experienced on our platform of choice. I don’t think writing that is falling into the trap it’s easy to end up in with major games that hit console first: declaring in salesman-like fashion that they’ll of course be better on PC by default, in a manner that sometimes feels a bit like you’re trying to convince yourself that you’ve not paid more than a pre-RAM crisis console buyer for nothing.

I’d never consider playing Cyberpunk 2077 in anything but first person on PC. GTA 6, from what I’ve played thus far, could be the next uber-detailed open world I spend hundreds of hours taking in the sights of, ideally through the eyes of a highly dangerous and highly stylish operator on the prowl for lucrative underworld opportunities.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, I love Charles and yes, that would be something that I would be interested in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as Inside the NBA’s latest season on ESPN continues, questions continue to swirl around the show in regard to its future. Longtime co-host Ernie Johnson has officially confirmed his aims to leave the show at the end of this season, and colleague Charles Barkley apparently plans to do the same. There’s been a lot of discussion regarding who might replace the beloved sports commentators, and Barkley recently pitched his successor. While it’s a solid pick, I’d admittedly prefer to see another seasoned pundit take over Barkley’s post.

Sources indicate that barkley – also known as “The Round Mound of Rebound” to some – is definitely someone who loves to speak his mind. So it doesn’t surprise me at all that he’d have thoughts on who might be able to take his place on Inside. The former Phoenix Sun was recently quoted as saying he didn’t believe anyone but fellow ex-player Jalen Rose could replace him at the desk. That comment was brought up to Rose when he was interviewed by Front Office Sports (as seen on YouTube) and, when asked about the job, he stated this:.

In a recent development, I love Charles and yes, that would be something that I would be interested in. The one thing I learned about this business is everything isn't transactional. If Charles Barkley is going to say into a microphone that you're the person that he feels like should replace him, you can't write a check for that. Even if it never happens. And so, for him to say that, it's priceless. I'm so very gracious.

In a recent development, the notion of Rose taking over for Barkley is actually quite reasonable, considering his resume as a broadcaster. He’s not only served as a fill-in analyst for Inside the NBA for years now, but he’s also taken on hosting duties for ABC/ESPN over the years. I personally enjoy seeing Rose when he appears on Inside, and his relaxed demeanor usually serves as a firm counterbalance to others on the dais like the vivacious Barkley or Shaquille O’Neal. With that remarked, there’s another recurring analyst I’d love to see join the show instead.

Inside has welcomed plenty of insightful and entertaining guest hosts over the years, from the cool Vince Carter to the wise-cracking Draymond Green (who has a rivalry with Charles Barkley). Someone who, for me, has always been a welcome presence on the show is Chris Webber, who’s been appearing on the show for years. He obviously has plenty of broadcasting experience, and he’s a wealth of knowledge when it comes to basketball. I’d say the show would be lucky to have him full-time.

It has been revealed that again, though, this isn’t to say that Jalen Rose wouldn’t be able to do the job effectively. There may actually be a reality in which both players end up on the show full time by next season. However, that’s assuming ESPN is looking to bring on two former players and not get another non-ex-player analyst to specifically fill the void that’ll be left by Johnson.

It has been revealed that to be honest, it may also behoove me not to get too ahead of myself right now, as the season is still young. Also, while Charles Barkley’s retirement claim is seeming more likely, he hasn’t remarked much more about it in the wake of Ernie Johnson’s announcement. We’ll just have to wait and see what happens and how the producers choose to proceed should Barkley leave the fold along with Johnson.

Check out Inside the NBA when it returns to NBA on Wednesday, November 25 amid the 2026 TV schedule.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that GTA 6 has a ton of unique weapon variants all with their own names and mods.
  • The Assassin Nipper is at the south tip of the eastern island in the Permit Keys.
  • Use Focus Mode to find the hidden cache for the Assassin Nipper .38.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that GTA 6 has a ton of unique weapon variants all with their own names and mods. They're all special custom builds of stock guns and weapons with unique skins, but some of them are way more worth the trouble to hunt down than others. You'll find some of them easily—every Ammu-Nation has a unique gun sitting out for you to buy. The best unique weapons are a little more hidden. There are treasure hunts and easter eggs and a whole lot that you'll grab by fighting your way through a gang hideout.

The Assassin Nipper is at the south tip of the eastern island in the Permit Keys.

Use Focus Mode to find the hidden cache for the Assassin Nipper .38.

It has been revealed that this is the easiest unique weapon to grab right at the start of the game and totally worth the boat ride to grab it. There isn't even any combat to get to it, like many of these other uniques. The Assassin Nipper comes with a suppressor attachment, which is a really expensive mod to buy early in the game. Pick it up as soon as you've got free range in Key Lento from an old shipwreck in the Permit Keys near the military base location.

According to recent reports, another great Chapter 1 snag is this sniper rifle at a Kingfisher hideout. The combat to get it is minimal (don't get between that tiger and its prey) so it's easy to pick up early. It's a bolt action that can't equip a silencer, so it isn't exactly a stealth tool, but it can help Jason pick off gangsters in a hideout before even going inside. It comes with a stock and a basic dot sight.

In a recent development, A variant of the Vom Feur V5FC, found in Port Gellhorn at a Kolt gang hideout. It's up on the top floor of the motel by the La Cascara Motel safe, so you pretty much have to complete this illegal operation to grab it. I recommend coming up the south stairwell that's less guarded and hugging the outer walkways to get most of the way to the loot room by stealth. It's worth it though. The Scrapper is a silenced longarm SMG fairly early in the game with an extended mag and a flashy paint job.

This Duke Carbine variant doesn't have a suppressor but it is quite high accuracy for a full auto assault rifle with a heavy stock and 7" pistol barrel mod. The Kolt 556 is easier to smash and grab than the Scrapper, though. You've got to fight in and out of the Kolt stash house, but it's a small joint so it's not too hard to get away clean. It's in a gun case on a kitchen table near the safe full of pills.

Letter from the Editor(s) #21: That game everyone is and isn't playing, and how we report on AI

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hello and welcome to an unusually not-Supporter exclusive ed letter, its paywall laying unbuilt so we can exchange some Real Talk with as many RPS readers as possible.
  • It has been revealed that S'been a weird one, hasn't it?
  • It has been revealed that the question of how to cover GTA 6 editorially is one we've spent months back-and-forthing over in meetings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hello and welcome to an unusually not-Supporter exclusive ed letter, its paywall laying unbuilt so we can exchange some Real Talk with as many RPS readers as possible.

It has been revealed that S'been a weird one, hasn't it? The biggest game release of a generation, a bonafide cultural event that's touched everything from the highest reaches of government to B&Q adverts, and yet Grand Theft Auto VI's lack of a PC version has kind of given it the feeling of a well-budgeted fireworks display going off outside your bedroom window. For me, anyway.

It has been revealed that the question of how to cover GTA 6 editorially is one we've spent months back-and-forthing over in meetings. Even if you consider "It's too substantial to ignore" a cop-out argument, the likelihood of it eventually coming to PC - based on historical precedent - is practically certain, making it at least partially fair game. At the same time, no, it is not 'a PC game' in its current form, and enthusiastically plastering the front page with coverage of something most of our readers probably can't play – with, say, a launch day liveblog, or a 100-hour-review-that-isn't-a-review-honest – would just be mad.

I'm quite happy with what we ended up with: continued but not excessive coverage of developments around the game, ongoing reporting on Rockstar's labour problems, and several consecutive days of irreverent posting about the other open-world crime games you can (or shouldn't) play. Why, then, was this restrained approach on the editorial side paired with near-blanket GTA output from our guides team?

The answer to that is the same answer we've been giving to anyone who's asked why RPS previously went as hard as we did on Baldur's Gate 3 or Starfield or Elden Ring: site's gotta eat. It is almost impossible to overstate how important guides are to the survival of a mostly-free games website, or frankly, how much better Ollie, Jeremy, Callum, Dion, and all our guiding 'lancers are at keeping the lights on than the rest of us. An example, which hopefully won't get me in trouble with the higher-ups for sharing 'business intelligence,' is that my piece on Derelikt - one of the most conventionally RPS-y features we ran during GTA 6 launch week - attracted nought point five percent of the eyeballs as Guides Gang's list of GTA strip clubs.

Some sites would look at that and think, well, guess we ought to stop writing about scratchy indie games and focus entirely on megablockbusters. We never have. Our way might create a bit of a parallel reality, where a section of the site does treat GTA 6 like a live PC game, but when those guides effectively fund, support, or otherwise enable the more diverse and offbeat editorial operation, you can't convince me it isn't the best way that's at the moment feasible.

Industry observers note that somewhere we can do better, however, is how we cover AI - genAI in particular. To start with, I'll temporarily yield the ed letter writing yoke back to Julian, who's on holiday but did send me this for inclusion:.

We've recently seen an ugly blow up in the comments under a series of articles on RPS and I wanted to address it now rather than wait until I'm back at the start of December.

It has been revealed that on November 10th, we published an article about House House's use of AI in the development of Big Walk. The article drew a huge amount of responses in the comments under the piece and also on social media. This is something we are seeing increasingly around anything to do with AI use in game development. There are entrenched camps on both the pro and anti side of this technology and anyone trying to talk between those positions is liable to get attacked. I want to address that but first I want to offer an apology.

The writer of the article took a comment under the piece and shared them on social media, portraying members of the RPS community in a negative light and inviting criticism from their followers. This came from a place of defensiveness – the conversation under the House House piece had become particularly heated and the writer was becoming the target of several abusive messages – but it was unacceptable to disrespect our commenters and readers in this way. I can only apologise for those who were hurt by this, especially those who were trying to be a moderating voice in the comments. Much as it is not acceptable for commenters to aim abuse at a writer (and I have banned the commenters who did this), it is not acceptable for an RPS writer to do this to a commenter.

It has been revealed that I have already spoken to the writer and they are fully aware of their mistake and the hurt they have caused and they won't be doing it again. I hope in time those who were hurt by this can feel comfortable returning to RPS. If they would like to talk any more about what happened, please do reach out to me by email (I will be back at work on December 7th, and I can respond to emails then).

Now, onto the tenor of conversations about generative AI. I recognise it has become far too aggressive in the comments. It has gotten to the point that it feels as though anyone who doesn't vehemently and explicitly attack the technology is treated as an enemy. I've not got involved in policing this and so by ignoring it I have allowed it to grow. I can only apologise for the hostile environment this has fostered and that our community have had to endure.

Industry observers note that I must admit I am unsure how to fix it entirely. But what I am going to try is writing articles that more openly discuss my own views on generative AI. As you may have picked up from some of my pieces this year, I've been talking to developers about their AI use and opening those conversations with examples of my own. A few years ago I was strictly against this technology but I don't find it so simple anymore. Hopefully by being more open in how conflicted I am about this tool, it will allow for more nuance in how we talk about it and that will help in the responses to other articles.

Once again, I am deeply sorry for the hurt we have caused members of the RPS community in recent weeks, I will try my utmost to make sure it doesn't happen again.

I'd add, in response to suggestions I've seen that RPS could enact a side-wide policy or charter on how we discuss AI, that directives like this tend to be non-starters. Fundamental to RPS is the idea that whoever comes and goes, everyone who writes for the site has the freedom to use their own voice, to express their own opinions. This obviously doesn't extend to getting involved in Internet slapfights or personal insults, and as Edwin has noted under a recent AI-tinged story, a consequence is that our output doesn't always follow a consistent editorial stance. Still, I feel that's a price worth paying for maintaining something that, to my eyes, has always made RPS special - if sometimes a little chaotic. And, despite our recent need of the ban button, the vast majority of our readers are smart and mature enough to grasp that different writers might have different views and interpretations.

For example, I don't think I'm as open as Julian to the use of genAI in games development, to be totally honest. Machine learning can and has done cool, unproblematic things for games-related tech and hardware, as well as more 'serious' business like medical imaging. But I'm yet to see anything out of contemporary genAI that outweighs its combined problems with environmental impact, poor output quality, unauthorised scraping of creative and technical works, its applications in producing misleading A/V material, and even the physical safety of impressionable chatbot customers. To say nothing of the fact that Google's embrace of genAI search results presents an existential threat to sites like RPS, regardless of how many guides to finding Skunk Ape (???) we produce.

All that stated, I do agree that we - all of us, fans and haters alike - would benefit from chilling out, and trying to navigate the matter with a little more thoughtfulness and a little less dunking. In keeping with the aforementioned editorial freedom, I can see myself writing less about genAI, not more, though on the occasions it does come up, I will try to articulate my opposition to it more deliberately.

It has been revealed that I'm also profoundly disinterested in anointing myself AI Cop, rushing to banish every confessed Claude user to the stockades; I don't have to make excuses for (or give my Advent Calendar votes to) games that adopted genAI, but if it's a matter of choosing targets, there are bigger fish to fry than individual indie games. As far as the comments go, we still only want to police actual bad behaviour, not any particular AI viewpoint, so hopefully we can join each other in this temperature-cooling and remember that "Be excellent to each other" isn't just an Eighties film reference.

To end on a jollier note, thanks to everyone who followed along with the RPS 100, another Not GTA highlight of the past week (and, indeed, 2026). I reckon this was one of the best, most vibrant lists we've done in years, owing in no small parts to the contributions of Sin, Oisin, and Jeremy P. You can vote right now for the RPS 100 Reader Edition, and our insatiable lust for ranking games will also manifest in the imminent 2026 RPS Advent Calendar, for which the reader-run Guessing Game is already open - with free RPS Supporter subscriptions as prizes. Which you might need, as future ed letters will be back as Supporter exclusives. Look, we're not made of nudity explainers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Banjo-Kazooie - the iconic Rare platformer starring an absent-minded bear and the sassy red bird he carries in a backpack - has been on hiatus for years, but a new Activision job listing has raised hopes for a new game.

In a LinkedIn post advertising a 'Product Manager, Emergent Franchises' role, the publisher wrote that it's "home to iconic gaming franchises including Call of Duty, Crash Bandicoot, Spyro the Dragon, and now… Halo, Age of Empires, Sea of Thieves, and Banjo Kazooie.".

In a recent development, "Become part of the team working on building, growing, and shaping many of these franchises," the listing goes on. "As a Product Manager, you will serve as the publishing product lead for an upcoming premium console & PC title, driving the product from concept to launch.".

Sources indicate that if you're scratching your brain trying to remember when Activision took control of the beloved platformer, well, it happened during Xbox's last massive internal shakeup. Amid the mass layoffs and studio divestments, Xbox also made some drastic changes to its corporate structure - Halo, World's Edge and Rare were all slotted under Activision's supervision.

Rare's 40-year history includes almost too many notable games to list, but the internal rejig presumably put Activision in control of games like Conker, Viva Pinata and Killer Instinct, alongside the aforementioned pirate hit Sea of Thieves and Banjo-Kazooie.

The job post is by no means confirmation that a fresh Banjo-Kazooie game is in development, but it is the only series named here that can be considered dormant, perhaps hinting that Activision has plans to revive it down the line. Crash Bandicoot 4 and Spyro: A Realm Beyond lay out a pretty good blueprint for its return, I think.

The last properly fresh game in the series came 18 years ago with the Xbox 360's Banjo-Kazooie: Nuts and Bolts, a surprisingly good physics-driven vehicle construction sandbox.

Since then, Banjo and Kazooie demonstrated up as a playable fighter in Super Smash Bros Ultimate. More recently, a fan-made PC port and an Evercade Double Pack have kept the series chugging.

Recent findings suggest that composer Grant Kirkhope was slightly more hopeful about the prospect of a Banjo-Threeie back in September. "I do know of like three companies that have actually physically pitched to Microsoft or to Rare about making another Banjo-Kazooie game, and I don't think anyone was successful," he noted at the time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 17-year-old girl who had been missing for more than a year was rescued and returned home by the FBI after a friend she made while playing Among Us, and his mother, were able to track down her location and pass it along to law enforcement.

Sources indicate that landon Tresp told the BBC that he and the anonymous girl "kind of just clicked" when they started chatting online while playing Among Us. She eventually told Tresp she was a runaway who'd been held against her will for more than a year. After learning more, Tresp, 16, told his mother, Khristina, about the exchange; she was initially suspicious, but after speaking with the girl directly on Discord and reading reports of her disappearance, she took action, asking for a piece of mail or document with a full name on it, which the girl provided.

Sources indicate that with that, Khristina began digging into tax and property records to find relevant addresses, which she then used to find photos on real estate sites. She revealed the photos to the missing girl on Discord, who picked out the one where she was being held; with that information in hand, Khristina contacted the girl's mother on social media and spoke to her briefly on the telephone, and also received a call from the FBI asking if she could confirm that the girl was still alive.

"I stated: 'I have; I video chatted with her, I've seen her'," Khristina told the BBC. "And she goes 'Oh my God, I cannot believe any of this'.".

Sources indicate that the kidnapped girl contacted Khristina the following morning, after her alleged captor, 39-year-old Adam Hunter Harmel, had left the house. In a conversation monitored by the FBI, she said she'd met Harmel on social media, where he'd pretended to be disabled and offered to pay her to help him get from Utah to Oregon. When he picked her up, however, he threw her phone into a river, then drove her to Oregon.

The girl told Khristina that she was kept in his basement and forced to sleep against the wall in his bed, while he kept a knife under his pillow to prevent escape. He gave her a mobile phone that wasn't able to make calls but could connect to wifi, which is how she was able to play online and eventually reach out for help.

While Harmel was out, law enforcement began monitoring his street and house; when the moment came, police had Khristina tell the victim that it was time to make her escape. She was able to leave the house safely and into the custody of state troopers, while Harmel was subsequently arrested and charged with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity.

A social media post by the Salt Lake City FBI confirmed the outcome, although the crucial role played by Landon and Khristina Tresp was omitted: It indicates only that "the FBI and the Rich County Sheriff’s Office have been actively investigating this case for more than a year and pursuing every lead received from across the US and in other countries.".

Recent findings suggest that A separate Department of Justice press release, however, acknowledges that "on Nov. 1, the FBI received a tip about the possible location of the minor victim and that the victim met Harmel on a social media application in May 2025.".

Khristina and Landon have remained in daily contact with the girl they helped rescue, and they're trying to arrange an in-person meetup as well. "Sometimes we just sit on video chat, just so she knows she has someone that cares," Khristina mentioned. "She was on video last night when I cooked dinner …it's nice to know that when she has a bad day or a bad moment, she can call me right away or call Landon right away. She's doing great for what she's gone through.".

As much as many would love for it to be true, AI is not capable of taking over translation duties for a game. Those that use it often receive complaints regarding the low-quality results; something that’s unsurprising considering translating hundreds of thousands of words that weave together into a cohesive story is a delicate and nuanced art, and an unaware technology that’s prone to making mistakes is unlikely to succeed. Even with human oversight, the results still reek. And if you remove even that guardrail? You may get something like Muv-Luv Girls Gaiden, which has just put out an English-language version consisting of in-game text declaring its refusal to translate “explicit sexual content.”.

In a recent development, the Muv-Luv visual novel dating series is perhaps unlikely to be on the radar of any but the most hardcore fans outside of Japan, but within the country the eroge franchise is hot property. Girls Gaiden is an idle RPG spin-off from a two-decade-old franchise that’s evolved from real-life tales to mecha action and alien storylines. Though its international exposure is mostly limited to a few anime adaptations in the 2000s, the series has maintained a niche audience in Japan thanks to regular new entries and a deluge of spin-offs. With Girls Gaiden, these spin-offs have expanded into the realm of gacha games.

It has been revealed that the game was released in 2025 in Japan in two distinct packages, one version broadly designed for all ages, the other an explicit version that keeps with the franchise’s adult roots. But the controversy surrounding this game only began earlier this week with the release of the English translation. As confirmed by a Japanese-language notice on the gameâs Steam page, certain translations for the game have been completed using AI tools. As fans soon discovered, this consisted of little more than inserting dialogue into AI tools and dropping it back into the game unchecked. The result is a game filled with countless lines of the AI pushing back against the localization requests, with statements like âI canât provide a translation for explicit sexual content.â.

âWhat the hell happened?â was the response of one player. The game has received a Mostly Negative response on its all-ages Steam release, with most of the reviews specifically citing the translation quality as a key issue.

Notably, developer Moedoki last year stated it would consider using AI translations if the technology could produce âtranslation quality to a level comparable to that of native translators.â It seems they decided to move ahead with it regardless.

  • Feder was leading Take-Two when GTA 4 debuted, so he certainly saw the "controversy around GTA," as he tells GamesBeat.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the popularity of Grand Theft Auto once stoked fears that the world's children would be induced to violent behavior and lives of crime, but GTA 6 seems to have courted far less controversy than its predecessors. Former Take-Two CEO Ben Feder believes that the series' edgy reputation still benefits Rockstar, even as it's become the most mainstream entertainment product in the world.

Feder was leading Take-Two when GTA 4 debuted, so he certainly saw the "controversy around GTA," as he tells GamesBeat. "In a way, it still has a bit of that patina that it uses to its own benefit, that gritty patina. But at the end of the day, it’s a completely mainstream game. It's the most mainstream game you can get, because it’s the most popular game.".

It's hard to argue otherwise about a game that sold more than 32 million copies before it even released, earning nearly $4 billion in launch sales. Rockstar's boasts that this is the biggest entertainment launch in history aren't mere bluster. The game's success "warms my heart," Feder indicates.

In a recent development, "I can't remember the last time you saw something where everybody around the globe – everybody, millions and billions of people – was as excited as for the release of this game launching day and date across the globe. It unites people geographically and demographically. I think it's what this planet needs.".

Recent findings suggest that these days, Feder is a managing partner at Tirta Ventures, a venture capital firm specializing in funding AI-driven game development. Predictably, he's big on the technology's future, comparing it to how GTA itself was created, when "new types of technology enabled new kinds of entertainment.".

Industry observers note that GTA 6, he argues, "may be the last of its kind. Not the IP. The IP isn’t going anywhere, and neither is the creative talent behind it. In fact, they're more powerful than ever. And there will be room in this fresh world for handmade games in the old style. But for the most part I think the industry is about to embark on a new way of developing and new types of experiences enabled by technology. It’s something that my firm is very much focused on in terms of what’s possible and what’s going to change.".

#108918. EA Sports FC 27 to resurrect John Motson with help from generative AI, because apparently football games need someone yelling about goals from beyond the grave

📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

EA Sports FC 27 to resurrect John Motson with help from generative AI, because apparently football games need someone yelling about goals from beyond the grave

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in today's instance of a sentence I never thought I'd write, English football commentator John Motson has followed in the footsteps of Darth Vader.
  • EA revealed Motson's resurrection for FC 27 to the BBC, with the deceased commentator's voice being made up of combination of old recording sessions and generative AI.
  • "My dad was the least technological person in the world," Motson's son Fred mentioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in today's instance of a sentence I never thought I'd write, English football commentator John Motson has followed in the footsteps of Darth Vader. In the latest instance of a game featuring a dead celebrity's voice reanimated with help from generative AI, EA Sports FC 27 will soon have Motson offering words about passes and shots that clank off the bar despite him having died in 2023.

EA revealed Motson's resurrection for FC 27 to the BBC, with the deceased commentator's voice being made up of combination of old recording sessions and generative AI. The publishers got permission from Motson's widow and son to do this, and told the BBC they'd not have gone ahead if Motson's family - whom EA have paid an undisclosed sum for the rights to use Motson's likeness and recreate his voice - hadn't been on board.

"My dad was the least technological person in the world," Motson's son Fred mentioned. "Till his dying day, he had a typewriter on his desk. So I don't think he would have quite understood what the AI was doing technologically - but I think, on the other hand, he was always really keen to get involved in these kinds of projects.".

Sources indicate that EA senior game design director Mat Prior mentioned AI has been used for the likes of lines in which Motson talks about modern players who don't feature in the old excerpts of him calling games. You'd think that might've been the point at which EA began to question why it's necessary to resurrect Motson for the purpose of commentating on games featuring a number of players he might never have watched while he was alive, meaning we don't know what unique calls he might have made in response to seeing them strut their stuff. Alas, it seems that wasn't the case.

"From a gaming standpoint, it's something we've used for many years - like machine learning to help drive animation systems and so on and so forth," Prior added. "It's not there to replace commentators in any way shape or form...there's certainly no future looks to replace anyone with AI." It's worth noting EA already use genAI to replicate the voices of some living commentators with their permission, with the justification given being that it helps cut down on the amount of work required to record hours of a real human saying different player names with different inflections.

Industry observers note that motson served as a commentator on FIFA 96 through 05, but looks to have been absent from the series since that point aside from briefly popping up for a return in FIFA 19. So, aside from that late 2010s one-off, Motson hadn't been part of one of EA's football games for about two decades prior to this AI-enabled resurrection for FC 27. I'd argue that makes it a lot more difficult to make the case for this use of genAI. It's not like the tech's being used to help maintain continuity with a voice that's always been part of the series' furniture, as is the case with Witcher 3 devs CD Projekt Red's modification of Geralt's Polish voice via genAI in the Songs of the Past DLC following actor Jacek Rozenek's stroke. In that case, the actor was also alive to give his direct permission.

Whether families or estates should be able to permit the use of AI cloning on the voices of actors or performers who didn't give written permission for it while they were alive is a matter of much contention. Actor Peter Caulfield, who's been arguing for greater protections against AI voice cloning through a campaign called Save Our Voices Now, argued in the BBC piece that it should only be allowed in cases where living people have signed deals to allow it.

Personally, I think games should probably do without genAI-fuelled celebrity ressurections, especially in scenarios where there seems no pressing need to do so. Even Tupac's likeness being used without any AI bollocks in RGG Studio's upcoming historical beat 'em up Stranger Than Heaven feels unsettling. AI Motson will be added to FC 27 as an optional commentator on November 26th.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toby Fox has given eager fans an upgrade on the development of Deltarune Chapter 6 and Chapter 7 - the Undertale follow-up's final two episodes.

According to recent reports, "Chapte 6 is progressing well," he wrote in a new blog post. "The game is now a structurally complete draft that can be played from the beginning to the end. All the maps, events, and battles exist. (Although there's still one optional event which is dragging out a bit…)".

While the bones are supposedly all there, Fox explained that he and his team still need to knock out localisation, testing and polishing. "Much of the game looks complete… but, some important scenes and details are still undercooked in their presentation, so it's going to take a bit longer before we can really move to full-on testing.".

Deltarune Chapter 6 was previously described as a slightly shorter episode that should hopefully set up the game's finale quite nicely. Despite being on the smaller side, Fox said he understandably doesn't want to rush development and "would like it to be as good as possible.".

And since Deltarune's next chapter is almost past the finish line - at least, in some respect - that means certain members of the team have already moved over to Chapter 7.

Sources indicate that "Well, we've only just started," Fox continued. "I read out the events and dialogue of Chapter 7 to the team. However, just when the story reached a critical moment, I stopped reading… I told my team they need to complete more of the game before I tell them what happens. Everyone agrees it's more fun this way".

"Unlike every other Chapter, I actually feel like I know what I'm doing this time, so I have a lot of confidence.".

In a recent development, deltarune's been on a long journey to get here, but, thankfully, the end is finally in sight. Deltarune debuted as a free download all the way back in 2018, a second chapter then dropped in 2021, the next two debuted together four years later, before the arrival of the most recent Chapter 5 this year.

Industry observers note that we don't know exactly how long Deltarune's last two chapters might take, but the good news is that it's already been a pretty fantastic game for years. Here's hoping those loose threads don't dangle for much longer.

We're just a couple weeks away from Marathon's Symbiosis update, a hefty overhaul patch that's aiming to inject some juice into the shooter's live service appeal with the addition of PvE roguelite and Team Deathmatch modes, new weapons, and even a social hub for hanging out with fellow runners and testing guns at the firing range.

Industry observers note that and that's all great. But today, Bungie dropped a newly introduced cinematic that presents its strongest argument for why Symbiosis should have our attention: You can play as a terrifying, sports-car scarlet robot samurai with a sword arm and jet legs.

While Bungie previously revealed Bishop, the upcoming runner shell arriving with Symbiosis, in the upgrade's first gameplay trailer earlier this month, the new cinematic provides a strong sense of the power fantasy it's trying to capture. By which I mean Bungie clearly wants you to feel like a nightmarish apex predator. Like a xenomorph if a xenomorph was bright red and had cool space guns.

Industry observers note that as the trailer progresses, we watch as a team of runners is steadily cut down by a Bishop shell's unflinching onslaught: First, one of its members is culled after taking one of Bishop's throwable hacking knives to the neck, which seems to disrupt the target's functions. The next is blasted out of midair while trying to zipline away to safety. The third is hounded by autopistol fire into a position where they can be conveniently pounced on from above.

But the trailer's peak moment happens as the Bishop prepares to loot one of its kills and is winged by a bullet from a nearby Rook, who evidently hoped to clean up after watching the whole fight pan out. This is proven to be a mistake, because the Bishop settles into a crouch, extending a plasma-edged sword blade from between its knuckles and engaging the jet thrusters in its calves.

You know that thing in samurai movies where a swordsman does a lunging slash, leaving the body of his opponent to realize that it's been cut down behind him? It's like that. But with robots and jet propulsion. Marathon's going to have iaijutsu, is what I'm saying. Something for us all to look forward to.

Marathon's Symbiosis patch lands on December 8.

I am not the Ironclad, nor was meant to be; am an attendant lord, one that will do to bind a necro, Exhaust a scene or two, advise the Regent; no doubt, an easy tool, Defective, glad to be of use, Politic, Silent, and Impervious; full of high synergy, but a bit obtuse; at times, indeed, almost ridiculous— almost, at times, the Fool.

Industry observers note that it has been a while since I played Slay the Spire 2. I return to find the forums full of grief concerning a recently introduced sixth character - a minstrel of sorts, dressed in carpets, who shoots arrows out of a harp.

The short version is that the Fool was wildly overpowered when Mega Crit added her to the early access deckbuilder's beta branch, with a base arrow-shooting mechanic that lets her dish out at least 21 damage in her first turn, and a Repeat Shot card that allows for upwards of 80. She ain't so vicious anymore, because they've just released a "mostly Fool-centric" patch that nerfs a couple dozen or so cards.

It's not all nerfs – they've buffed Cho Chorus, Quietus and Show Off, among others, while reworking Tune, Flourescence and Rapid Shot. There's a fresh Rare card, Optimism, which exhausts all Sadness in your Hand, while drawing a card for every card exhausted.

According to recent reports, some context: Sadness is a special colourless card, earned by way of cards like Mourning Blow. It remains in your hand between turns and can't be played, making it an immediate hindrance, but you can transform it and use it as fuel for certain cards. Just like real sadness! Best of all, you can turn it into Joy, which grants you Energy. Reading about this complex neurophysical alchemy is making me tired. Shall I give the beta build a go? Do I dare to eat a peach? Are you sick of ham-fisted Prufrock references yet?

Industry observers note that read the full patch notes here. The Fool is an interesting creation, eyebrow-raising damage output aside, and I look forward to her addition to the game's main Steam branch. She can play various flavours of music to modify other cards.

I do like a weird bard, and I broadly approve of the practice of releasing fresh early access characters with all the sliders pushed to max, waiting for the cacophonous whining to reach a certain pitch, and then jocularly chopping back their stats. I should get back into Slay the Spire 2. I just have to play [redacted] first.

It has been revealed that roughly half of the studio (513 out of 1051 developers) is now working on The Witcher 4 ahead of a planned 2028 release, with 199 developers working on Cyberpunk 2, a slight increase from earlier this year. This has led to the team working on the studio’s Witcher spin-off, right now titled Sirius, shrinking slightly from 84 developers to a team of 60, while a newly introduced IP known as HadarÂ remains in development with a smaller team.

Paradox grand strategy Afterworld has a wasteland band mechanic that sounds worryingly like a continent-sized game of The Sims

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Much like a huge dust cloud gradually resolving into an army of skull-painted bikers, Paradox's post-apocalyptic grand strategy game Afterworld continues to take shape in the course of developer blog posts.
  • Each band has needs, satiation of which makes them feel more motivated and thus, more willing to follow your orders and work for the good of the tribe as a whole.
  • It appears to make for some alarming diversity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Much like a huge dust cloud gradually resolving into an army of skull-painted bikers, Paradox's post-apocalyptic grand strategy game Afterworld continues to take shape in the course of developer blog posts. The latest Parablog digs into what I think is one of the game's most interesting aspects – you don't control one single unified civ. Instead, you amass a motley tribe by befriending, conquering, or otherwise assimilating a range of individual wasteland bands.

Each band has needs, satiation of which makes them feel more motivated and thus, more willing to follow your orders and work for the good of the tribe as a whole. Some of the needs are more generic – for example, shelter, nutrition, hydration, medicine, social standing, and security against threats. Others are bespoke, shaped by Custom - another in-game social metric - and by that band's origins.

It appears to make for some alarming diversity. For example, you could have a band that are full vegetarian, and excel at foraging - they won't even eat dried insects, the hippies! You could also have a band of cannibals who have a literal Human Flesh consumption gauge. I see nothing in the latest dev diary to forbid you from assimilating both the cannibals and the vegetarians. Let's, er, not seat them next to each other at the next council meeting, unless we're really running low on finger food.

Sources indicate that "All needs can scale by band size, level or other game state elements that make sense," the developers write. "Another thing to keep in mind is that different bands will value different needs depending on who they are or recent events. For example a band that’s experienced extreme hunger will get more motivation from nutrition, while a band on the council will expect to get more standing because of where they are in society, not just because of who they are.

"When all of these things come together, you are invited to pick which bands are important for your tribe’s goals," the blog continues. "Those bands are the ones you will pay the most attention to motivate. When you look more closely at what those bands actually want you will find narratively and systemically immersive choices to make. At one point a band may care about food because you are facing a famine, but then rumors of some dustland horror beyond the tribe borders scares everyone into caring more about security and downplaying their previous preoccupation with food.".

Sources indicate that the most "work-in-progress" part of Afterworld's band motivation system is managing the potential gulf between an individual band's needs and overall tribe policy. You can, for example, put troops in settlements to make bands feel "dominated", which "increases their motivation, bypassing the needs, and allows you to run parts of your tribe with the stick, while others get the carrot.".

The developers are "still iterating on this side of the system, but the intent is for such tactics to [offer] various degrees of sustainability for your tribe, depending on your set up and who your bands are". If you try to coerce a band, you run the risk of them blowing up in rebellion as and when the stick is removed. "This can result in cool moments like you taking down a bigger threatening tribe who’s keeping their lower classes under control through forced medical sedation, but it all comes apart when you find a way to sabotage or raid the source of the sedatives," the blog explains. Seems very fiendish! There are many points of comparison here with other Paradox games, of course. Before writing this piece, I asked Mark for his take on Afterworld based on many hours desecrating the Catholic Church and/or wine trade in Crusader Kings 3. He observed that the game sounds a bit like playing the unlanded leader of some adventurers in CK3. Myself, I wish I could make some precise references to the Europa Universalis series, but our resident expert Brendy (RPS in peace) left many moons ago to found some appalling indepedendent website or other. So I'm going to swing for the fences and say this feels like a continent-scale game of The Sims, except with groups of irradiated and tattooed, neo-Bronze age pillagers instead of smooth-faced burbanites. For the most informed appraisal of all, here's Julian's chat with Paradox about the game's procedural history generation - it writes you a latest apocalypse for every playthrough.

  • I'm a member of noted corner of the overall fandom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the prayers of Final Fantasy old heads were finally answered this year with the release of Final Fantasy Resonance, a particularly retro-feeling entry in the franchise. Between the real-time battle system and 2.5D aesthetic, it's a throwback in the best way, and fans embraced it wholeheartedly, so much so, even the devs were surprised.

"I think the action-oriented and 3D Final Fantasy games are wonderful too," Keisuke Nakashima, producer on Resonance, told Game*Spark, as translated by Automaton. "But I was surprised to see just how many people, not only in Japan but overseas as well, are eager for the kind of Final Fantasy they remember from back in the day, with classic turn-based battles and pixel art.".

I'm a member of noted corner of the overall fandom. Much as I enjoyed the huge, sleek main entries, my heart yearns for games that look and feel like the SNES installments, but with contemporary flavor. That's what Resonance delivers.

"We figured it was something we ourselves would enjoy, and that there would be players out there who’d feel the same way," Nakashima adds. That's always a good starting point, and the devs figured correctly, although there was some concern over just how much it stood out amid the slate otherwise.

"I expected opinions on it might be divided," Hiroto Furuya, director of Resonance, commented in the same interview. "I think the fact that a game with such an unusual background has been embraced by so many people is a positive for the industry as a whole, and I’m personally very happy to see it.".

You and I both. Fans of the long-running role-playing juggernaut have had plenty to enjoy the last while. Besides Resonance, Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth continued the trilogy's blockbuster redux of the classic game, and Final Fantasy Tactics: The Ivalice Chronicles resurrected a fan-favorite for modern systems.

Sources indicate that final Fantasy Resonance is itself a top-down remake of aspects of Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, a mobile game from 2015. I'm willing to bet most who checked out this version glossed over the original. It's probably safe to get moving on a follow-up that draws from further parts of the narrative in Exvius.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A PC version of Grand Theft Auto 6 - one from unofficial sources, at least - may be closer than we thought.
  • Industry observers note that "The exe is out.
  • Hours later, the recompilation modders and hackers part of the Project Leonida Discord server - the current hub for all GTA 6 recompilation efforts - posted footage of the game booting up on PC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A PC version of Grand Theft Auto 6 - one from unofficial sources, at least - may be closer than we thought. After suddenly returning last week with a near-full build of the Xbox version, notorious leaker CyberLeek has now posted the missing piece they intentionally held back: the game's executable (.exe) file.

Industry observers note that "The exe is out. Always free. An early Christmas gift from CL," CyberLeek reportedly wrote, as relayed on Reddit. "The torch passes to the open source re-comp and emulation projects.".

Hours later, the recompilation modders and hackers part of the Project Leonida Discord server - the current hub for all GTA 6 recompilation efforts - posted footage of the game booting up on PC.

Industry observers note that in just a matter of hours, modders - with the help of Claude AI - managed to turn the leaked Xbox build into a PC port, of sorts. In this Reddit video, you can see the game boot up to the initial setup before hitting a black screen. The build is clearly not yet playable, though Eurogamer has not directly verified those claims.

Shayder, one of the lead developers on Project Leonida, mentioned in a since-deleted post on X that we should "expect a lot of static recompilation work to be done soon." On the project's Discord server, they later clarified that it could take about a week for the build to reach a playable state on PC.

According to recent reports, as for CyberLeek, the leaker is still soliciting donations for a secret project "for the gamers", adding in the build's readme file, "Nobody has to give anything, and every release stays free either way. But every donation is a vote for more of this, and so is every trade of the token.".

Rockstar has not announced a PC version of GTA 6, but the manufacturer has historically released its games on PC several months after their console debut. In October, a report noted GTA 6's PC version would arrive in the first quarter of 2027, an unusually short gap between the console and PC releases.

These latest recompilation efforts, however, may force Rockstar to speed up development of the PC version. Though the recompiled build may never reach the level of quality or stability of an official port, many of those eager to play the game on PC likely wouldn't care.

#108904. Company of Heroes 3: Operation Torch review - moments of barely held-together chaos squandered by mechanical scripting
