📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first HBO Lego Harry Potter sets have been revealed, and they're remaking some classic kits... but fans aren't all enthused by the result.

After being teased earlier this year, the initial wave of Lego Harry Potter kits based on HBO's latest series revisits some old haunts; the lineup includes the Gryffindor Common Room, the Hogwarts Express, and Privet Drive. These include new designs and minifigures based on the TV show, but there are obviously similarities to what we've seen before – and that seems to be a sticking point for some. In a Reddit post discussing the sets, the top comment notes that they "they look like bootlegs of the originals lol.".

Industry observers note that while there's positive feedback as well (particularly toward Privet Drive's faux-Tudor design), I'm finding just as many negative responses on social media after a quick look through the likes of Instagram. These sets are clearly dividing the community, and I can't imagine it's the reception Lego was hoping for. Here are the kits themselves:.

Industry observers note that the Gryffindor Common Room is a constant throughout the Potter stories, so it makes sense that Lego would remake it here in its new HBO form. This one is made up of 738 pieces, comes with five minifigures (Harry, Ron, Hermione, Parvati, and Lavender), as well as lots of little details on almost every surface.UK: £79.99 at Lego.

This is probably the most unique of the sets, as the faux-Tudor exterior is quite different from the old movie version. The kit has 545 pieces and four minifigs to go with a brick-built '90s car – Harry, Uncle Vernon, Aunt Petunia, and Dudley. UK: £54.99 at Lego.

According to recent reports, what with Harry's first trip to Hogwarts being such a pivotal moment in the story, it makes sense that the Hogwarts Express would feature as a major latest set. This is just the latest in a long line of models recreating this train, and while the engine itself is practically identical, the HBO version of the platform looks like it includes a little cafe waiting area that we've not seen before.UK: £89.99 at Lego.

In a recent development, the final set to be revealed thus far is a BrickHeadz kit, recreating characters in a larger scale. This one has Harry, Malfoy, and Hagrid presumably while they're wandering the Forbidden Forest in detention. It's made up of 380 pieces.UK: £22.99 at Lego.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most prominent figures of the so-called Bluenami was not a candidate on the ballot, but rather a Twitch streamer and political commentator: Hasan Piker.

According to recent reports, this year Hasan was involved in dozens of races across the country, campaigning for progressive candidates like Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed. But you’re probably more likely to associate Hasan’s name with what other people have had to say about him—from Fox News commentators to more established members of the Democratic Party.

Sources indicate that hasan regularly courts controversy on both his hours-long Twitch streams, where he’s said things like “America deserved 9/11,” and social media, where he’s written that Hamas “is a thousand times better than” Israel. He claims he’s often taken out of context, and that his audience knows what he really means—and where he stands. In his mind, he’s a leftist provocateur, maybe, but one who understands the importance of working-class values and electoral strategy.

While Hasan has walked back some of his more inflammatory language, his rhetoric raises the question: Is he a liability to the cause he champions? Or is he successfully reaching the critical audience—namely, young men—that helped elect the wave of progressives poised to take office in January?

It has been revealed that with 2028 on the horizon, I wanted to know how Hasan thinks about his growing platform, and if he sees his role shifting in the media landscape. What responsibility does he have to his viewers and to the candidates he supports? And does he regret any of those past statements?

We also got into the DSA’s more extreme positions and how to make sense of them; why he thinks the Republicans put his thirst trap on the jumbotron at their convention; and how he, a self-proclaimed socialist, thinks about his own money.

Mark Guiducci: Hasan Piker, welcome to Fair Game.

Hasan Piker: Very excited to be here.

Thanks for coming. Hasan, you are more online than just about anyone. You spend at least seven hours a day streaming. You reach tens of thousands of people at a time on average, and it’s all in the channel that you control. I’m curious, what are you doing here with me today? Why are you showing up for a show with a legacy media publication? What’s in it for you?

Sources indicate that well, I saw the clips and everybody looked really good. The lighting was perfect. I saw the Dari[aliza Avila Chevalier] clips, I saw Ta-Nehisi [Coates], and I was like, I got to get in on that.

In a recent development, yeah. So shouts out to the team. You guys did a phenomenal job lighting this up. It looks very cool too.

In a recent development, okay. We’ll take the compliment.

But the serious answer is, I mean, I reach an audience that obviously does not watch television, does not read legacy publications at all. And I want to show people that read Vanity Fair that I am not a terrorist.

Industry observers note that right. Which brings me to my next question because—.

Yeah, exactly. That would be the name of the episode. You’ve been everywhere this year, and you became this kind of bogeyman for the right, who probably have never heard you, watched your stream, or heard anything you’ve said out of your mouth. They’ve just heard quotes repeated by news anchors. And not even just for the right, even for some on the left. And you played this interesting role because you were a surrogate and a media figure and then a media figure covering the media as well. I want to spend a little bit of time talking about how you see your role. And to start, do you consider yourself a journalist?

Okay. Because it’s like you present this interesting newly introduced type of figure. I was thinking about how you’ve done an interview with CNN, you’ve done interviews with MS NOW, but they don’t have you on as much as I would expect them to.

I have some thoughts, but I wonder why you think that is.

In a recent development, I think I’ve pissed off a bunch of executives over there, because, in my experience, there are plenty of amazing reporters and journalists and producers that I know that work at all of these newsrooms, right? But from what I have seen, the masthead has a very different editorial slant than sometimes what the reporters want to cover.

Because they talk about you a lot.

They talk about me a lot. And also I’ve never been invited on any of these outlets as a pundit either, which is also strange because, as you also pointed to, I don’t just operate as a campaignster. As a matter of fact, that’s something I did very briefly and I did not like it at all. I’m first and foremost a commentator…. I do have the capacity to do journalism at times. I’ll do interviews with candidates. I’ll go out and—.

Well, candidates I like. Sometimes I do interviews with candidates I don’t like or I’m unsure about as well. The problem is most of the candidates don’t want to come on if they know I’m gonna cook ’em. Like Gavin Newsom, I have had feelers out to get him on the broadcast.

In a recent development, I have. Gavin, Gavin, come on the show. I am a taxpaying California resident. I’m one of your constituents. You want to be president in 2028, you’re gonna have to be able to talk to people like myself.

Recent findings suggest that all right. So, Hasan, this cycle you were involved in some way in, by one count, 48 different candidates’ races, and AIPAC and pro-Israel groups spent about $101 million in those races. I feel a lot of hope. Hopefully it’s not going to be short-lived. But I feel very excited for the first time in a very long time, after 10 years of some of the most odious politics that we’ve seen from Trumpism, from MAGA. We finally saw a real sea change through electoralism. People truly have had enough with Trumpism.

I wouldn’t be so certain because I feel like if there’s one controlled opposition party that is capable of breathing life back into MAGA, it would be the establishment Democrats. So I’m a little bit worried, but it’s very clear that people are truly fed up.

According to recent reports, all right. So there are a couple of different narratives that are coming out of the midterms right now. Rahm Emanuel, for instance, is touting this as a victory for moderate Democrats, saying that they ran 21 points above Kamala Harris. The DSA, meanwhile, is claiming that American voters have “emphatically endorsed socialism.” Other pundits are saying that these massive gains have nothing to do with the Democrats and are actually about the war in Iran and high gas prices. Sources indicate that I mean, I think this is not even a new debate. This factional battle has existed within the Democratic Party and perhaps—.

Yeah, but the progressive wing was always really fringe.

Industry observers note that and now we’re talking about—I don’t know if 50/50 is right. I don’t want to use numbers, but—.

I think it’s a testament to our success, especially in the midterms, that there are a lot of people who are trying to protect their comfortable sinecures and are outright panicking. And all of that completely sidesteps the reality that the vulgar Bernie-ism of 2016 was echoed through every single candidacy, every single campaign all across the country, from the obvious Berniecrats like Abdul El-Sayed to even people like Roy Cooper, who in the past were very moderate, very centrist. And he still is a center-right figure, which clearly works in North Carolina. But even he was railing against data centers, billionaires, the uncertainty surrounding AI. I mean, this is left populism. And that rhetoric, one could say, was deployed in the past by even the likes of Bill Clinton and Al Gore.

Industry observers note that but for some strange reason, there was a turning point in 2016 where the Democratic Party adopted this strange role of defending the corporate class and defending the elites and took ownership over, I guess, defending these institutions overall. And these institutions are worthy of defending, for the record. However, from the perspective of the masses, if the government is failing them, if these institutions are failing them, then they wanted someone to break it. And that was obviously the right populism of Donald Trump. And break those institutions, he surely did. And we’ve seen the devastating results of that.

So you credit the progressivism with what happened on election night?

Absolutely. I mean, there’s certainly local moderation on issues, right? Because James Talarico went from saying “God is nonbinary” to “we need to defend our transgender brothers and sisters, our neighbors,” which is, again, insanely woke for Texas, or just in general, right? There are far more conservative figures in the party than James Talarico’s current position on the trans problem.

Sources indicate that okay. But sometimes the way that you run—oftentimes the way that you run needs to be different than the way that you govern or lead once you’re there. Do you think it is productive to continue pushing some of the farther-left ideas once they get to Congress? Or is pragmatism and getting things done, you know, defining things that are really achievable and sticking to them as a bloc, as a group, and pushing them over the line— when you’re talking to some of these winners, are you talking about [that]?

I think if I could speak to the entire incoming freshman class or the entire caucus—.

Recent findings suggest that I would say, be bold, be brave, and obviously immediately implement accountability. Investigations are an absolute must. This is what people are demanding. After the economy, the second concern, the biggest concern, is corruption. The second term with Trump has been unbelievable. I mean, look, I’m Turkish. I’ve seen corruption in the Turkish government. I’ve seen corruption and tracked it and talked about it all around the world with different governments. I’ve never seen anything like what the Trump administration has done because of how flagrant and in your face it was. So you’re calling for subpoenas and investigations.

I think impeachment, especially for Trump, is probably the last thing that I care about. I mean, I want these guys to go to jail. Let’s be clear. If they’ve done the crime, they need to do the time. I don’t think anyone is above the law. We have to restore law and order. So I’m a law-and-order Democrat. And I know that sounds something very different in Washington, DC, or in general. I think when politicians say that, they mean, like, punish the poor for minor crimes. I’m talking about punishing the wealthy for their corruption, for their major crimes, because they’re the ones who are robbing people blind.

According to recent reports, but, you know, a lot of people would say that impeachment would be a distraction. So I guess what I’m saying is, if you had to choose three agenda items that the Democrats are agreeing on and they’re going forward with—you already said subpoenas and investigations.

Recent findings suggest that what else? What are the other two that in the first year you really want to see happen?

I think it’s virtually impossible [with] the current DOJ to—they’re not impartial, right? I don’t think that we are going to move the needle on actual criminal investigations before the Democrats win the White House in 2028. But all of this is building up for that moment. And for that reason, I think we need to talk about affordability—and not just simply talk about affordability, but also explain how we’re going to solve the affordability crisis through a comprehensive legislative agenda. And one of the major issues around affordability that is oftentimes discussed as a separate thing, but it’s not, is health care. And the Democratic Party’s approach to health care has been lackluster. Even though Americans obviously overwhelmingly trust the Democrats with fixing health care or solving the problem with health care, the reality of the matter is, while the ACA was a fantastic improvement to what existed previously, it’s not enough, and we have to move the needle in a healthier direction. We have to push for a single-payer health care solution.

I’m perfectly fine with that. I’ve joked about that for years ’cause he’s so invested. He’s such a petty despot and so narcissistic that—.

Yes. I have pitched this over and over again on my show. Look, you win so massive with Donald Trump if you go to Donald Trump and you say, “Look, Obamacare, not the best, right? Now you get to destroy Obamacare and you get to build something else in your name. We call it Trumpcare. It’s single-payer. It’s Medicare for All.” I think he would do it.

Look at this. Bipartisan collaboration.

Industry observers note that yes, I’m pragmatic. I’m bipartisan.

It has been revealed that all right, so let’s take a step back. You were talking a second ago about how Talarico was woke. And on November 4, Twitter, formerly known as X, was amazing. Memes, jokes, you know.

Recent findings suggest that I see what you did there. Yeah. We flipped it back.

Yeah, we flipped it back. With the Democrats’ victory, the idea that woke was back, do you think that’s true? Do you think that we’re going to see, culturally, the return of this idea of woke? And do you think that’s a good thing for the Democrats?

In a recent development, yes. I do think that the pendulum swing was an inevitability. I talked about this quite a bit. I saw the early warning signs when [Joe] Biden won. That was one of my major warnings that young men were going to go back to the Gamergate era of very far-right politics because the Biden administration was not delivering. And what ended up happening with this anti-woke narrative, this culture war that the Republicans had seemingly won, that they presented as a mandate, right, was some of the most odious commentary, some of the most vile rhetoric that anyone had ever seen.

Definitely. The idea of woke now, though, I'm just curious—being politically correct or precise in one’s language was, for a time, an outward indication of being a progressive or maybe even being a good person in culture. Do you think that’s still the case?

In a recent development, I mean, I’m progressive, so I think so, but I’m a little biased. But I will say this: I think that there were certainly social excesses, which is ironic because this whole Woke 1.0, 2.0 distinction, I feel a little responsible for in the discourse because I jokingly used to say—.

According to recent reports, yeah, now I’ve joked about that too, and now journalists are reaching out to me being like, “Do you think Woke 3.0 is real?” I’m like, “I’m joking, guys. It’s not serious.” But here’s the thing, there is a little bit of sincerity there. I think one of the things that I routinely criticized during that 2016-to-2022, 2023, era of, I guess, Woke 1.0 was the social excesses, the maximalist demands, the inability to understand that people are complex and don’t have the same lived experience that everybody else has. I always would get so frustrated because we on the left say America’s a white supremacist country, and yet we don’t ever reflect on what kind of social conditioning comes along with that. So that if you do actually hear someone engage in a microaggression, for example, that we have to be a little bit more understanding and try to ease them into the conversation.

According to recent reports, and on the other side, people will say, “Oh, that’s normalizing this kind of behavior. It’s unacceptable.” And I totally see the other side of that argument as well, but I think, especially if you’re campaigning or especially if you’re building a movement, you do have to be a little bit more understanding and not be so hardheaded and assume that everyone has to agree with you from the jump without you making a convincing case as to why you might be correct.

Sources indicate that okay. All right. So we’ve talked a lot about what you think about the political landscape, but I want to talk also about your role in it right now and going forward. Having mentioned that, on the political-ideological side of things, of course I am the furthest from all of those figures. I’m just talking about the form and function of it all.

Industry observers note that okay. So it seems like you’ve been recently the guy that progressives come to when they’re trying to run a primary from the left, but then when they get to the general or to office, maybe they don’t need you as much, or they have left you behind, or they distanced themselves from you. According to recent reports, yes. But the thing is, what I’m doing is too fresh for people to fully realize, to fully comprehend. So we talked a little bit earlier about your audience at the very beginning. You know, you’re an interesting figure for them. As far as the responsibilities that I have, I am very aware of them. I see myself as, in some respects, NPR for Zoomers. Yeah, that’s just a lot of pressure, though, because NPR has a whole staff of people that, [if] someone’s sick, someone can pinch-hit.

I mean, I’m fine living in that environment. I’m happy to do it. I’m happy to take on that responsibility.

It has been revealed that can I ask, what’s your personal life like right now? I mean, that is a lot of time on the air, and probably you have to read the news yourself too. So are you seeing friends a lot? Do you see your family a lot?

In a recent development, I keep my private life private for obvious reasons ’cause there are a lot of insane people out there. But yes, I do spend a good deal of time with friends and family. I have normie friends as well that are just completely removed from the world of politics and from the world of Hollywood, influencers, that kind of thing.

Do you think of yourself as a role model?

Sources indicate that in some respects, yes. I don’t think people should follow everything that I do to a T, but I definitely do see that. I think that’s a good influence.

Yeah, I think that is a good influence. You’re rocking a nice suit yourself.

Sources indicate that I bought this at a photo shoot for Days magazine. This stylist had pulled this and I loved it.

I literally was like, “I’m buying this from you.” And then since then, she’s been pulling stuff for me.

According to recent reports, can I ask, are you having fun? Because it seems like you are, but then what we were talking about before, with the way that you might feel abandoned—and especially the past few months, this cycle, has it been fun?

No, it has not been fun. I don’t think it’s great to be called a terrorist and lied about and slandered endlessly with the hopes that this could potentially tank the Democratic Party’s chances of bringing about accountability to this fascist administration. I did not enjoy that.

And I certainly also did not enjoy the fact that I was kind of left out on my own a little bit, where—of course I got a lot of support from the movement, DSA, and the wonderful slate of candidates that we worked with, but I’ve never had institutional backing. And as a matter of fact, there was a lot of anxiety from the institution that is the Democratic Party. So all of its loyal servants were going on TV and being like, “He’s a horrible person who needs to go away,” over and over again. So that didn’t feel great. ’Cause there’s always negative polarization when Trump attacks someone and the Republicans attack someone, but if there isn’t any backing from the liberal side, even from a partisan perspective, then that complicates things. All of a sudden you’re like, Okay, well, who’s on my side now? I have nobody to push back.

You’re playing this game where you try to find the worst quotes that you can and frame them as negatively as you can, and then attack candidates that might not even know the context behind some of these words. Bernie was, I think, the best, ironically enough, at dealing with it when he was asked by Abby Phillip. He called me a radio man, which is funny. He’s been on the show, still doesn’t know what I do, which is fine. That’s unc, that’s grand-unc. But he basically said, “Look, everybody says silly things. I mean, he talks for thousands of hours. He’s a radio man. And not only does everybody say silly things, but ultimately there’s a reason why he has such a passionate fan base, because we agree on the broad spectrum of issues that he advocates for, and so do all of his fans. So to reduce someone to a couple of choice clips is obviously going to never give you the full picture.” I mean, he didn’t use all those words.

It’s not about being a person; it’s about being a cudgel, just something that you can use as a counterbalance.

I don’t think liberals, and even the left broadly, [are] ready for how to deal with that because we’ve never really had a person like me in the past. I mean, the Republicans obviously have three to four decades of this, coming from William F. Buckley all the way to Rush Limbaugh and Charlie Kirk and numerous other far-right figures, that they know how to brush this aside. I mean, JD Vance, when asked about his affiliation with Tucker Carlson, will be like, “He’s my friend.” And that’s it. That’s that.

Sources indicate that okay. So you’re streaming most of the day, you’re reacting to news in real time, and just even by your own admission, you’ve noted some—I think you said “silly things.” I would say some pretty extreme things along the way.

According to recent reports, and I know you’ve walked back past statements. “America deserved 9/11”—how many times have you heard that this season? Because I think regret is different than “wish I said differently.”.

It’s a tough one. I mean, look, I probably will regret things that I will say in the future as well. It’s virtually impossible for me not to say things—.

Yeah, it is, but it also isn’t because I have apologized and taken back some of the things that I’ve said and apologized for how I worded or framed things. But do I regret it? I mean, I feel like I’m stronger as a consequence of all of those experiences at the same time, so I don’t know.

Do you feel like someone in your role has a different responsibility with their words or their public platform than an elected official or even a journalist?

Okay. But you also said that you are a role model.

Can you parse that a little bit?

Yeah, absolutely. It goes back to the space that I occupy and what I try to do with it. Right? I don’t think that I am, at least to my audience or anyone else that’s paying attention, doing anything that’s remotely politically as toxic as the way that the current systems operate. The rude behavior that I demonstrate is what people get frustrated by or what they attack, but—.

Yeah, I am vulgar, for sure. But I think the systems of violence and oppression that people are subjected to [are] far worse than any vulgar thing I could have ever said. And we kind of saw this dynamic play itself out on the campaign trail as well. And I think the finality of it all came with Haley Stevens, when she decided to lean into the “Hasan Piker is such a problem that I'm leaving the Democratic Party and endorsing the Republican platform.” [That] was, I think in some respects, a wake-up call because it forced everyone to go, Wait a minute. No, those guys are actually far worse. What are we talking about? Right? Because at the end of the day, Donald Trump is not only vulgar, but he’s also violent. And sure, I’m vulgar, but ultimately I’m fighting for social justice. I’m fighting for people who are dispossessed, people who don’t get heard at all. I’m trying to offer them a voice, a platform for their frustrations, and communicate their desires, their anxieties.

Do you think the vulgarity actually helps you with your audience? Because if they’re young men, men in their 20s, it’s like the edgelord vernacular.

Recent findings suggest that certainly, but I don’t do it for some tactical purpose. I do it because that’s just who I am.

I mean, I always say, look, if you go after marginalized people, vulnerable populations, and you bully them, I’m gonna bully you. Someone has to do it.

For what it’s worth, you’re being very civil right now.

Oh yeah. I mean, this is a very different format. I am very different in these sorts of professional settings than I am on my own broadcast where I’m offering off-the-cuff commentary on these hot-button concerns.

Is this more performative, or is that?

I would say this is more performative.

I’m much more civil here. I’m not going to talk in the same way that I do on my broadcast. But here’s the thing, I can’t be fake on my broadcast. And I’m not even saying I’m being fake here. I’m just being nice.

Industry observers note that but what I will say is this: A lot of people don’t realize that this is an interactive medium. Most people think, when they see a clip, especially if it’s chopped a certain way—.

Yes. Most people think this is my preproduced, prescripted statement ’cause that’s all they’ve seen from the Jake Tappers of the world. They don’t realize that I am offering extemporaneous commentary on a breaking news story in real time, without a production team, while simultaneously—.

In a recent development, no. While simultaneously duking it out with anonymous accounts. What is the one thing that everybody hates on Twitter and everywhere else on the internet?

Recent findings suggest that the comment section. My entire platform revolves around yelling at the comment section, and the comment section is yelling back at me.

We’ve got to get you a practice.

In a recent development, but that is like, I’m in the zone. That’s when I’m in the pocket. I love being in that space.

You’ve been outspoken about distinguishing criticism of Israel from antisemitism, but do you think that there are moments when legitimate anger at Israel can create an environment in which antisemitism becomes acceptable, even among people who would never consider themselves antisemitic?

And what responsibility do you think you have, given the size of your audience and your influence with it, to call that out when it happens?

According to recent reports, I do call it out when it happens, and it happens quite frequently. It’s not a secret that antisemitism has exploded in the Western world, especially after October 7. And that is why I take special care and consideration when talking about this problem in particular. Whenever I talk about Israel, there’s always going to be some people who will be like, “Well, you know how the Jews are.” And I will always take the time out to explain to my audience, and to whoever’s saying an offensive statement or an antisemitic statement, why they’re wrong. And I think it’s key to do that, not because—it’s not like the canary mission of the ADL is gonna be like, “This guy that we have presented to you as a prominent critic of Israel, that we’re desperately trying to paint as an antisemite, has actually spent thousands of hours combating antisemitism and will continue to do so because he’s an antifascist.” They don’t want to present the complexity of that argument because, let’s be real, it’s pretty tough trying to defend Israel. It’s not an easy endeavor.

Can you think of a time when you contributed to that problem, not intentionally, but maybe through something you said and the way your audience responded?

No, because every clip that people post, or every moment that people have posted to point to this suspected antisemitism that I harbor, oftentimes is sandwiched between a comment that I have made leading up to it that completely destroys the narrative. The example I will present to you is the famous moment where I got disavowed by the entire Democratic Party. I mentioned something that I have said as an anti-Zionist for the last decade and will continue to say because it’s the truth: that Jews are not monolithic and that Israel should not be the responsibility of the entire Jewish population, and that anti-Zionism is not antisemitism; however, that forced conflation of Jews in Israel is increasing antisemitism. And they chopped it up and packaged it and turned it into this major media moment.

It has been revealed that so speaking of misinterpretations, you recently filed a defamation lawsuit against conservative commentator Scott Jennings, although you’ve noted you were very deliberately anti-litigation for a long time before that. So what changed? Why this suit? And who else are you planning to sue?

So what changed is the heinous nature of this defamation. It was definitely a bridge too far. I feel like there is a boundary that was crossed that I could no longer abide by. And there’s a level of defamation and slander that takes place in the political conversation, but what Scott Jennings did was so disgusting and so malicious that I had to demand a retraction. Snopes did an article immediately because it was so heinous. He claimed that I was on video advocating to lynch Black voters. I’ve spent my entire life fighting against white supremacy, and the fact that they maliciously edited this video to make it seem like I was in favor of something that I’ve always been in opposition to, something so heinous, a hate crime, was outright unacceptable. So I wish that it didn’t have to get to litigation, but for some strange reason, they decided not to respond to our request for a retraction and now we’re here.

Who else are you planning to sue?

I mean, there are a lot of people who have engaged in that exact same kind of defamation and slander. So whoever has participated in it should probably be on the lookout.

Okay. In the national chapter of the DSA, there are some pretty extreme platform positions that—I saw Mamdani answer these questions on Fox News the other night. I’m sure you did too.

And I'm actually just curious where you stand on some of them.

So here’s the thing with the platform in its entirety. I think the format itself doesn’t actually do justice to the program, to describe the program, and it’s almost impossible to explain it as an elected representative or a mayor in a hostile or contentious media environment, if you’re on Fox News or whatever. The problem, I think, with the program is, there are certain elements of it that I don’t agree with fundamentally, but it’s a democratically organized, democratically voted-on program that DSA members voted for. And the way I see it is, these are very, very long-term goals, and I think this is not talked about in mainstream media at all. It is a platform, but it’s more so a North Star that we are working toward. Designing society in a way that yields egalitarian outcomes. That we do away with certain systems of cruelty is an honorable goal, is a just goal, even if I don’t fully agree with some elements of it.

It has been revealed that I’m not a prison abolitionist; I’m not a police abolitionist. The reason why I don’t believe in that concept is because I think that these are necessary functions that must exist, but also must serve the people. Right now it doesn’t. It serves capital and that needs to change, that needs to be retooled. However, I also recognize that the current system that exists is far more ruthless, far more insane, even if we’ve normalized it, than even police abolition is. So from my perspective, if we look at where we’re at, the carceral state that exists, where America has 25% of the entire planet’s prisoner population despite only making up 4% of the overall population, and the recidivism rates that we have in this country, and the fact that we even have a private prison system in this country—that’s insane. That is insane by global standards. So it’s tough for me to sit here and say I oppose the DSA platform and program when I understand what they are trying to communicate.

It has been revealed that and also, I think what is the regular order of business right now is far more insane than even prison abolition. Even though prison abolition is far-fetched and I don’t agree with it, I think the best possible way to go about it would be to have an electoral program, the perceivable, the permissible, the possible, and then the long-term goals, the long-term agenda, ’cause it’s not going to be easy to run and try to win on a platform that is not only idealistic, but also does not reflect the current societal understandings of concepts. Because most people think cops are awesome, they can do no wrong, they’re heroes, they’re constantly fighting crime, and they’re stopping rapes from happening, and they’re diving in front of bullets, but that’s not the case. I wish that was the case, but that’s not the case. But people overall [have] a very positive attitude about policing as an institution.

Recent findings suggest that but there’s also quick and quippy ways to respond fast. I just told you I’m a law-and-order Democrat, right?

Sources indicate that immediately that signals something. Another thing that I always say about policing is, I want police to do their jobs. I think that, by and large, they have a profoundly important task that they have to accomplish. Their presence is supposed to invoke law and order. Their presence sometimes invokes lawlessness and disorder. That’s unacceptable. They’re very well paid. They have the best unions. Do your jobs better. That’s my attitude on policing. So it’s antagonistic, but it’s also a demand that I’m making from this institution that I truly do believe is important for society to function. That’s one way to tackle this concern in a way that Americans understand. I like to call it chudifying your commentary. Zohran does a very good job of libifying his commentary. He’s very liberal-appealing. I like to do the opposite. I like to chudify it. I appeal to the chuds. I speak from that tone and that language when I advocate for certain things.

According to recent reports, yeah, edgelord vernacular, sure. But it’s kind of like, whether we’re talking about abortions or whether we’re talking about transgender bills, like anti-trans bills, I’m like, I don’t want the fucking government getting involved in these affairs. What do you want? You want some creepy pervert to do penis inspection day at your high school? What are you, a pervert? Are you a pedophile? I want small government when it comes to this kind of stuff. And that is a way to argue from a perspective that I think right-wingers can understand.

Switching gears, we talked a little bit about suits for a second, but I want to talk about style more largely. So at the RNC’s midterm convention in September, there was a 25-foot selfie of you in underwear displayed on the jumbotron. How do you think about that?

It’s a strange thing because I wish I was as in shape right now as I was, because that was peak.

Thank you. But also at the same time, I’m like, Oh, I wish I looked like that right now.

Why do you think they’re so obsessed with your looks? What is going on there? How is that helpful to them actually?

It has been revealed that it’s not. I think about that quite a bit. I think…they’re gay.

It has been revealed that that’s it. I think they’re in the closet. There are a lot of Republican operatives that are just either gay or in the closet and haven’t been able to figure out how to communicate their desires. So they were just frustrated and confused. But there’s no other reason to have this pathological, this psychosexual, obsession where you’re like, “My opponent, this political opponent, is a dangerous guy. He’s a radical communist, Islamist, jihadist.”.

“And he’s also sexy. Look at him shirtless. Look at him shirtless.” Because I thought these guys were peak masculinity. I thought that’s what they were about. The Joe Rogan Experience, you know, Brazilian jiujitsu, and working out was supposed to be the thing in the right.

There’s nothing unmasculine about being gay.

Sources indicate that I’m kidding. That’s not how they think of it. I know.

And not only that, but also, ultimately, why are they showing a shirtless photo of me where I look jacked?

Yeah. Okay. But it’s not just the GOP. Almost any coverage of you, including now this, includes a reference to your appearance. And I’m sorry we’re doing this right now.

Do you like it in some regard, or does it bother you?

Industry observers note that it’s attention. I like it. In the past, when people would approach me and be like, “Why is The Newly introduced York Times only talking about how you look and not talking about your ideas?” I was like, “Look, that is terrorism insurance.” If I’m getting into these legacy publishers and not being called a terrorist and instead being called a hot guy, I’ll take it.

In a recent development, okay. Okay. One last question about your looks. If Calvin Klein calls tomorrow and wants you to do the Houston Street billboard, are you doing it?

I would need to immediately get on a steroid regimen. I would need to look like Kumail Nanjiani before.

I mean, yeah, I would do it. Why wouldn’t I do it?

Okay. I wonder, with your audience, because there are a bunch of young guys looking up to a guy who’s maybe slightly older than them, looks like they might want to look, is that homoerotic at all?

It has been revealed that but I do have a fairly queer community as well. We do a census. We do a yearly census. Fourteen percent of my audience is trans, which is obviously much higher than the American population.

What are some other demos that would be interesting that we wouldn’t expect?

Well, the classic ones are obviously—it’s like 60% white men under the age of 35.

You perform best with all the people that Vanity Fair performs worst [with].

Industry observers note that I think a lot of mainstream outlets are really bad at captivating the attention of young men in particular. That’s probably part of the reason why people are always fascinated with this group. They’re trying to understand it.

Industry observers note that what about you captured them? How did you do it?

Sources indicate that I was a young man at some point, and I also have the same interests, and I think that’s part of it. And I also speak—going back to the crude, the language that I deploy, the vulgar language that I deploy, it’s like I speak like a normal person. I speak and get angry in the same exact ways that normal people do.

According to recent reports, all right. Hasan, what’s your attitude toward money? How do you think about money?

Recent findings suggest that for me personally, it has a corrosive influence, I think. It has the capacity to make you unbelievably out of touch. It’s something that I think about quite a bit in my own personal experience. I was a very stubborn person with air travel. Even when I had a little bit of additional income, I refused to pay the extra for the economy-plus seats.

In a recent development, I’m a major dude. I’m 6’4”, I can’t fit in the seats, and I would still. It’s a point of pride. Until one day I was put in a business class seat for some kind of business travel. And at that point I had enough money to purchase business class seats on my own, and I was like, I’m never looking back.

Industry observers note that you were ruined. You were ruined.

It ruined me. It completely ruined me. So now—.

Tina Brown notes that the private plane ruins people, that when you see how that works, it’s over. Hook, line, sinker, people are done.

That corruption is almost—she doesn't say this, but I’m interpreting that it’s almost inevitable after that.

Yes. I think that every instance of financial stability or financial freedom that I’ve gained has made me more out of step with the struggles that I used to experience and the struggle that everyday people experience. And I think you have to always be in touch. Especially in my line of work, you have to understand where people are. On the other hand, though, it is editorial freedom, because I have been able to maintain complete editorial control, complete editorial freedom, because I am completely unbought, completely unbossed, completely unshackled. There have been numerous instances where I’ve obviously had contracts with Amazon and stuff like that because I know I need to play ball also to make sure that I am a reliable team player so they don’t deplatform me. However, there have been so many instances where people have come to me with tremendous sponsorship opportunities.

Polymarket is one that I talk about all the time. [For] 2024 election night, their opening salvo was a million dollars just to have their ticker on the side. I said, of course, no, because I feel like it’s deeply unethical to be sponsored by a gambling manufacturer, a prediction market, while, you know, you’re engaging in news commentary. But I know that if I did not have that economic freedom, that financial freedom, I would’ve probably had to think about whether or not I’d make this ethical compromise.

So Calvin Klein would be an exception.

Calvin Klein’s fine. I mean, I take sponsorships every now and then, like gaming companies and stuff like that. If Rockstar came to me and were like, “Grand Theft Auto VI is coming out. We want to sponsor a stream,” I would fucking love that.

Some people have a number that’s like their retirement number, at which point that’s all the money they need. They close up shop and call it a day. I wonder if you have a number after which you think it would be unethical to accumulate any more. What is the maximum amount of net worth or income that you could generate after which you would feel it’s morally reprehensible?

It has been revealed that great question. I have no idea. I’ve never thought about it like that because there’s no world in which I will reach that number. But all the revenue that I generate goes immediately back into this broader project. It allows me to be able to travel around the country. It allows me to be able to hire people on a moment’s notice if necessary. So that’s the way I see it. I don’t have an unethical number, but I think to each their own, because I don’t want people to hear me say this and then be like, “Well, you know, you’ve collaborated with Saikat Chakrabarti. He’s a centimillionaire. You’ve talked to Tom Steyer. He’s a billionaire.” I care more about what people’s actual advocacy is and if they’re real about it or not. And I think how much they pay into certain things can show that, for sure. But anything past the point of having—not your net worth, right, but anything past the point of just having $10 million, I feel like is insane. It’s like, What are you doing? Does that make sense?

Because you said you differentiate with net worth.

In a recent development, I differentiate it with net worth because everyone will say, “Oh, well, I have assets. I have stocks,” or whatever. But in general, if you have—.

The capacity to deploy—I feel like even $10 million is too much. If you have the capacity to deploy a million dollars into something, you’re done, you’re set. I think everything past that point is outright ridiculous.

All right. I want to look ahead to the future because 2028 is not far away, and I think all signs would show that you’re going to be a character in that cycle. So here’s the inevitable 2028 question: Do you think the public has met the 2028 candidate that you’ll champion yet, or do you think that person is still waiting in the wings somewhere?

It has been revealed that I mean, the top answer, obviously, since we’re doing this will-they-won’t-they thing, is AOC. Right? She is the one figure, I think, on the left that has the capacity to unite the base, and she’s competent, she’s charismatic, incredible progressive track record as a legislator, and—.

Who is moving more to the center.

Well, I think all that stuff is—it’s pragmatism. I don’t think that means that she is going to come out and be like, “I am no longer in favor of the same comprehensive policy agenda that I’ve sought to advance my whole life.”.

But it might mean that she wants to unite the base.

Yeah. But I don’t think you necessarily have to do compromise on the legislative front to unite the base. If I was being fully transparent, fully honest, or maybe a little harsh, my criticisms around AOC would probably be that she’s not aggressive enough and that at times she’s come across as perhaps a little too liberal, too woke, on social challenges in a way that is not appealing to broad subsets of the base.

Sources indicate that okay. Say AOC runs but loses the primary, and you’re dealing with Josh Shapiro or Gavin Newsom or insert centrist Democrat here.

What do you proposal to do? Do you urge your audience to get behind them?

Sources indicate that I don’t know. I don’t know what I would do at that point. I haven’t even thought about it because I don’t think I need to think about it.

I don’t think it’s even going to be a problem.

So, I guess AOC or not, how do you want to be involved in the 2028 election?

I’m gonna do what I did in the primaries and the midterm broadly, and hopefully we’ll have a slate of hundreds of democratic socialists that will be running in every district that will be bold, that will excite the base, and that will chart a different path forward for the Democratic Party by force.

Do you think that—we’ve talked a little bit about this toxicity of the brand of Hasan Piker, which has been burnished by the right and by some on the left.

In a recent development, do you think about trying to clean that up, as it were, so that you could be more helpful to whoever that progressive candidate is? Or is it more useful for you to be ethically pure, I guess, in your estimation and stay as the stick in the mud on the far left?

Look, I got to the point I got to by being honest and sometimes being hardheaded, being stubborn, but always saying the truth. And that policy’s not going to change. So I say, if this is considered too toxic for politicians to take advantage of this platform, then they’ll lose. Because my goal is not to change myself. My goal is to change politics. I want American politics to be more responsive, not only to our demands, but also reflective of our anger as well. I truly believe that we are in the moral majority. People who look at the current system and say, “This is not helping,” people who look at their insurance premiums going up and say, “We need to change this,” that is a morally righteous fury that people feel, and there is a great deal of time and effort spent on mainstream outlets, legacy publishers in the media broadly, to try to quiet that frustration. I believe that I have a more honest approach to the matter, and that is precisely the reason why my audience continues to grow as their audience continues to age out or diminish.

I want to end on a slightly different note. I want to do a lightning round with you. I’m gonna say a series of names and I just want you to give me word association, the first thing that comes to your mind—just don’t say their job. It’s too boring.

Oh, there’s so many directions I can go with this. Do I joke? Do I fib? Do I say what I honestly think?

You just gave me a whole speech about being honest.

Well, on my broadcast, I joke and I call him the “sex panther” because he’s so uncharismatic, but I joke and say, “Oh my God, he’s so hot. He’s so charismatic every time he comes out and delivers this speech, finger-wagging speech.” But the serious answer, the one-word serious answer, would be corrupt.

Shit. Damn it. That works for Kim too.

I thought you were gonna say the same thing.

According to recent reports, I don’t want to repeat. I don’t want to repeat. Kim Kardashian, white feminist.

In a recent development, oh damn. I used “manlet” for Stephen Miller. Can I use multiple words for Nick Fuentes?

Sources indicate that yeah, yeah. Please give me money. Fund the DSA.

Ooh, a lot of deployment of the word “manlet” today. No, he’s ape.

Recent findings suggest that all right. Okay, to end, I want to do a round of the Proust Questionnaire. So this is the longtime back page of the magazine. They’re small but poignant questions that say a lot about you. So are you ready?

Okay. Hasan, what is your greatest extravagance?

According to recent reports, ooh, that’s a good one. I can’t say my house because I feel like it’s very expensive, but it’s expensive because of the housing market in Los Angeles. So I’ll say business class travel.

In a recent development, okay. What’s your most marked characteristic?

It has been revealed that I don’t know. Probably my looks.

That’s a good question. Let me think. I have to dig deep for this one. When do I lie? When I have to be polite.

Sources indicate that I don’t have any regrets. I mean, you asked me about the things that I’ve said, if I regret them. I feel like I have a policy of just bouldering through the pressure and just pushing through, no matter what happens, because there’s no use crying over spilled milk. So when things happen and they’re devastating, I think about it. I feel like there are different ways that I could have gone about things and how I manage them, but ultimately I’m stronger on the other side.

It has been revealed that I learn from it. I’m stronger on the other side because of it. So I don’t really regret anything.

When and where were you happiest?

Sources indicate that zohran victory party 2025 was peak. Even the Bluenami was really good, but I think that was so significant for me because it was the first time I had approached a campaign hands-on and played somewhat of a role in that victory. And I was surrounded by all these people that were door knockers that had worked on the campaign. They were coming up and they’re like, “Dude, I’m here, we’re all here, because I saw Zohran on your stream, and I was like, This guy is the truth, this guy’s the real deal. And then we knocked on millions of doors.” And I felt so proud. I felt like there was a real impact that my community had made in this race in some small sense of the word.

Hasan Piker, thank you very much for coming on Fair Game.

Today's Nintendo Switch Online upgrade finally introduces a feature players have been asking for since 2018

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There's been an exciting addition to the Nintendo Classics GameCube app today, as consumers have discovered a small - but oft-requested - change in the software's Version 2.2.0.
  • This new option arrived fairly quietly as part of an revision that otherwise introduced Wave Race: Blue Storm to the Nintendo Classics – GameCube lineup.
  • Recent findings suggest that why is this such a massive deal?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's been an exciting addition to the Nintendo Classics GameCube app today, as consumers have discovered a small - but oft-requested - change in the software's Version 2.2.0.

This new option arrived fairly quietly as part of an revision that otherwise introduced Wave Race: Blue Storm to the Nintendo Classics – GameCube lineup. That addition may have generated the most headlines, but it's this one little toggle that's getting many players exicted.

Recent findings suggest that why is this such a massive deal? Previously, the bordered image on the 4:3 aspect ratio games contained lots of little dots, and players complained that these were distracting at best, and casused discomfort on the eyes whilst playing at worst. Other players worried it would contribute to screen burn-in on older televsion sets. As part of the upcoming update, you can simply border your games with plain black - a tiny revision, but one that you can already see online communities celebrating. The player icon (another UI element that attracts derision) is still present, however, but as one comment summarises: "it's a step in the right direction".

According to recent reports, "Oh my gawd, I've been wanting this! I hate the checkered on the side, it clashed with every game I tried," says one social media user." Players have been complaining about these borders and UI elements since Nintendo Classics was introduced on the Nintendo Switch back on 18th September, 2018. So it's taken a good eight years for Nintendo to - finally - implement a change.

Industry observers note that in order to change the border yourself, you need to head to the game library selection screen on the Nintendo Classics app, navigate to the game settings, and locate the option to toggle this border graphic in the "Extra Elements Display" tab. Hit the button and - bang - you're done. At the time of writing, this option only appears on the GameCue app, and only on Switch 2, but people on social media are already asking Nintendo to enable it across the original Switch and other apps in the library, too.

It has been revealed that not everyone is happy with the 'slowly, slowly' approach Nintendo is taking towards implementing these changes, though. "Why can't we expect the full step with no graphic at all?" asks one irritated poster on Reddit. "Why do you have to deal with these half assed implementations for a paid deluxe subscription service?".

"Oh well, probably gotta wait another 10 years for the next improvement" says another. Another slightly more constructive user outlines what helpful additons might look like, noting that adding a "blurred zoomed in image of the game to fill out the background, or just extending the colors outward into the border, or maybe something fun like a CRT TV-looking border like the NES and SNES Classic had" would go a long way to make the retro experience better on the consoles.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • CD Projekt made its Q3 2026 financial report today, and there's not a whole lot to see: The Witcher 3 remaster was a big hit, work on Cyberpunk 2 and The Witcher 4 is ticking along, and everyone really liked Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2.
  • According to recent reports, perhaps understandably, a number of questions in the subsequent investors call put the focus on Grand Theft Auto 6.
  • It has been revealed that "Obviously, this is a call about us, not about Rockstar, but I do understand the connection here," Nowakowski mentioned when asked if The Witcher 4 will represent a technological leap over its predecessor comparable to GTA 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CD Projekt made its Q3 2026 financial report today, and there's not a whole lot to see: The Witcher 3 remaster was a big hit, work on Cyberpunk 2 and The Witcher 4 is ticking along, and everyone really liked Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2.

According to recent reports, perhaps understandably, a number of questions in the subsequent investors call put the focus on Grand Theft Auto 6. While CD Projekt joint CEO Michał Nowakowski didn't go too deep on the topic, he did say that the upcoming Witcher 4 will be comparable to GTA 6 in at least one way.

It has been revealed that "Obviously, this is a call about us, not about Rockstar, but I do understand the connection here," Nowakowski mentioned when asked if The Witcher 4 will represent a technological leap over its predecessor comparable to GTA 6. "Having said that, of course, I'm not going to make a deep dive and a full-blown review of GTA 5 versus GTA 6. But of course, we did look at the game. We did see the differences.

"Do we believe there's going to be a comparable leap between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4? I think so, yes. I mean, it's been 11 years. We are working on The Witcher 4 to make it significantly better looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game. So yes, you should expect us to make a much bigger jump between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4.".

Well, sure. As Nowakowski remarked, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt was released 11 years ago, and it'll be two more years before The Witcher 4 comes out—assuming it's not delayed, which would make it a rarity among CD Projekt games. It will also be the same number of years between Witcher 3 and 4 as spanned GTA 5 and 6. In the world of technology, 13 years is a long time.

Hell, just the upgrade from the original Witcher 3 to the remastered version that dropped earlier this year is notable:.

At the same time, Nowakowski said that while the GTA 6 launch was tremendously successful, CD Projekt Red doesn't intend to merely mimic Rockstar's approach when The Witcher 4 is ready to go: "Our games are different and the require a certain different approach, and we just do certain things differently than they do.".

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

He also remarked that while the release of GTA 6 has had an impact on Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk 2077 sales on consoles, he doesn't expect it to have a "material impact" on the company's Q4 finances for one obvious reason.

"You do have to remember that a lot of our players are also PC-based," Nowakowski said. "GTA has not launched on PC. We have not seen any impact whatsoever on the PC sales on engagement." And, he added, "on the PS5 and Xbox, it's not like our sales came to zero.".

Nowakowsi also said that GTA 6 hasn't changed CD Projekt's ambitions for The Witcher 4 and Cyberpunk 2: If anything, it's "an inspiration in many ways for our developers." And he's not concerned about its success pushing up development budgets, because CD Projekt's games "are not budget-driven developments.".

"I'm not saying that we don't care about the budgets. We do, and I'm pretty sure [Rockstar] did as well," Nowakowski said. "But you cannot make games like that having in mind, 'This is the fixed number of money I want to spend, and that's it. Otherwise, we're gone.'.

"They are ambition-driven developments and money is important. The budgets are not indefinite. That's not what we're saying. But the philosophy is kind of like I noted. And honestly, that philosophy has not changed for us because of GTA 6's release. It has just always been like that.".

Nowakowski's positive take on GTA 6 isn't too far off that of Cyberpunk 2 creative director Igor Sarzynski, who stated yesterday that he's suffering from "GTA 6-induced-open-world-game-dev-depression," although he rapidly clarified that CD Projekt is "doing something of our own, with a different unique flavor." (And that he wasn't being serious about cancelling Cyberpunk 2.).

seriously though i think we're doing something of our own, with a different unique flavor. GTA is impressive in a way all great art is, it expands what is possible, a captivating vision flawlessly executed.

The Witcher 4 is currently slated for launch sometime in 2028, while Cyberpunk 2 isn't expected out before 2030.

#108864. As Blizzard whacks one World of Warcraft: Forever gold farming exploit, it struggles to contain all of the alternatives popping up

As Blizzard whacks one World of Warcraft: Forever gold farming exploit, it struggles to contain all of the alternatives popping up

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • World of Warcraft: Forever is in the grip of a gold-farming bonanza, as Blizzard's attempts to curb them are met with a seemingly endless wave of alternative money-making methods.
  • Last week an exploitative method of making gold in the game was removed.
  • For one, it was the first time Blizzard has put a stop to a specific money-making strategy in Forever.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

World of Warcraft: Forever is in the grip of a gold-farming bonanza, as Blizzard's attempts to curb them are met with a seemingly endless wave of alternative money-making methods.

First, some context. Last week an exploitative method of making gold in the game was removed. The exploit involved repeatedly running the new Blackmaw Hold dungeon and promptly killing non-elite enemies which were - mistakenly - given better loot drops than they were supposed to have. This was taken out, and people exploiting this to extreme degrees were temporarily suspended and had trading blocks put on their accounts. In addition, gold gained this way was removed from their accounts.

This was a significant deal. For one, it was the first time Blizzard has put a stop to a specific money-making strategy in Forever. But in the days following Blizzard's action, other exploits have been discovered requiring similar action.

In a recent development, let's start with dungeon farming. In World of Warcraft, you are limited to entering 10 separate dungeon instances per hour before the game starts locking you out. This farming method is based around promptly entering these dungeons, killing the mobs for loot, leaving and resetting the dungeon, then rinsing and repeating. Do this 10 times and you've got a handsome payday.

Recent findings suggest that some players were running into the side entrance of the Uldaman dungeon to kill a specific boss, The Obsidian Sentinel, in a way that would take just a few minutes. So people were able to farm valuable boss loot and max the dungeon limit of 20-30 gold earned in an hour. This exploit has been killed, with Blizzard removing the loot from this boss to temporarily curb the strategy.

It has been revealed that this isn't without its challenges. Primarily, by removing the loot from that aforementioned Uldaman boss, several strong items had been removed for regular players. This included one part of the beloved Pendulum of Doom axe, which was unobtainable in-game until the loot was turned back on for the boss.

However, this is far from the only dungeon farming method. Players are now repeatedly farming non-boss enemies in the upcoming Krol'dok Stronghold to earn potentially upwards of 100 gold an hour. And presumably more people are looking for more exploits all the time. Blizzard, in turn, has had to halve the instance cap in World of Warcraft: Forever to five to attempt to get control of the situation.

It has been revealed that so that's the end of it, right? Well, no! While these instanced farms have proven lucrative, they are far from the only way of gathering vast amounts of gold. Already, players have discovered that by grouping and killing Furbolgs in Felwood, they can all pick up beads - seemingly another bug in the game. These can be exchanged for items, which in turn can be sold off to a vendor for a tidy profit.

Even if this gets patched, there are other 'valid' farms capable of turning a quick profit. You can, for example, kill turtles in Mount Hyjal and skin them for valuable leather and turtle scales, not to mention their meat and occasional trash to sell to vendors. Why is this valid while dungeon farms aren't? It raises the question: what makes a gold-farming method worth fixing?

In a recent development, it's a tricky problem. To defend gold farmers for a moment, the game has a history of gold farming that has been permitted. For years, mages have been blasting down dungeon mobs without fear of ban nor suspension. In response to the Blackmaw Hold fix, Blizzard said: "Finding efficient farming spots has always been a part of the game, and is how most players have earned their epic mounts since 2004. When a single location proves so lucrative that it overshadows all other sources, we generally adjust it to bring it in line with the rest.".

So the line appears to be the level of profit made from a particular farm. Though without this line being drawn explicitly, one wonders how gold farmers will know whether their strategy is safe or not. There is a culture around goldfarming that has existed since the game first released in the early 2000s. These aren't bad players. They aren't even naughty players, really. They've been a part of the game's culture for over 20 years.

At the same time, it's hard not to feel for the developers here. This is not the same World of Warcraft as the one players jumped into decades ago. Long gone are the days when a few guildies could accrue wealth with a humble farming method. Gold farmers are now equipped with the skills to efficiently harvest mobs with ease, and can promptly hop between server layers to access mobs quicker, and when a lucrative farm is found, it can be kept secret within Discord servers and run endlessly until Blizzard wisens up.

At the same time, the developers have to stay on top of this stuff. Already the in-game economy is getting more expensive as time goes on, and those who have taken their time to level with friends are facing fiscal pressures that those who rushed through it did not encounter. All the while, Blizzard has acknowledged that gold farming is a part of the game, and so the pressure not to cater to some good ol' fashioned hustling is doubtless weighing on their shoulders.

What will likely happen is this. Gold farmers will bounce around with the developers hot on their tails until finally the farms deemed unintended or exploitative are made untenable. That's when and where the line will be drawn. This will likely be a continuous problem as updates bring more potential money-making opportunities to the game, but it's safe to say there's an element of uncertainty surrounding the situation.

The big question is whether the events of the Blackmaw Hold suspensions put enough fear into the hearts of gold farmers to curb their exploitative habits? If it hasn't, do the developers have the nerve to dish out more severe punishments? Time, as always, will be the test of it.

According to recent reports, for those of you who aren't already max level and farming gold, or trapped up in Winterspring, grinding out Wintersaber Trainers reputation for no reason (me), it's worth emphasising that World of Warcraft: Forever does bring a lot of the magic of the original game back alongside quality of life changes. Give it a go, if you dare.

#108863. Why Kate Middleton's Return to William's Side Says a Lot About the Future of the Monarchy
